summary: The respondent assessee was assessed to wealth tax for the assessment years 1965 66, 1966 67 and 1967 68 (the respective valuation dates being March 31, 1965, March 31. The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the money lending investments. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and urged that as it maintained its books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interests on the amount lent investments could not be included in the wealth tax assessments. The Appellate Tribunal held that the judgment of the Orissa High Court was binding on it, and accordingly by a consolidated order dated April 3, 1972 it dismissed the appeals. In doing so the Appellate Tribunal followed "Commissioner of Wealth Tax Bihar and Orissa vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju (Orissa)(1), The Wealth tax Officer appealed to this Court. Dismissing the reference, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 3 of the Wealth Tax Act, wealth tax is charged for every assessment year in respect of the net wealth of the assessee on the corresponding valuation date. The expression "net wealth" is defined by cl. (m) of section 2 of the Act as "the amount by which the aggregate value . Of all the assets, wherever located, belonging to the assessee, on the valuation date, is in excess of the aggregate values of all the debts owed by the assessee upon the valuation dates. [310C] 2. The computation of the gross wealth of an assessee calls for a determination of his assets and debts as on the value date. All the assets of the assesee, bar those expressly excepted by the statute, are to be taken into account, and it is immaterial whether the assessee employs one system of accountancy or another. There is clear indication that the assets to be considered are not circumscribed by any consideration of the particular system of accounts adopted by the assesses. The assets are not confined to cash. Where the asset is an asset other than cash, its value is determined pursuant to sub section (I) of s.7 as the estimated price, which, in the opinion of the Income Tax Officer, the asset would fetch if sold in the open market on the valued date. In other words, it would be the estimated open market value of the rights in the property which constitute the asset. When we speak of the value of a property, on a legal plane we refer to the value Of the rights In that property. It is apparent that what accrues as a right also falls to be included within the assets. [311D E] 3. The reasons for defining the valuation day in terms of the last day of the income tax "previous year" stop there. The system of assessment, mercantile or cash or hybrid, is of no relevance for the purpose of determining the assets Of the assessee. That appears plainly from the definition or "net Wealth" which speaks of "the aggregate value".

The respondent was a Time Keeper in Beas Sutlej Link Project, Sundernagar. He was incharge of preparing the pay bills and other bills of the work charg ed employees of the project. It was alleged that he ma sie minded and prepared the pay roll pertaining to 'T ' Token of Central Survey Division, Sunder Nagar for the month of May 1969, even though Ash ok Kumar was not working in that Division. A bogus identi ty card in the name of Ashok Kumar T.No. 59 T at serial No. 10 on page 2 of the relevant pay roll was issued to him by the Respondent. The Respondent made this entry with ulterior motive to withdraw the pay of Ashok k Kumar for the months of May, 1969 even though as Ash ok Kr. was not in working in the Division. He made this Entry with ulterior motives to withdraw his pay for the period of May1969 even though he was not paid wages for three years in respect of Shri Sain Ditt a, Clerk. The Tribunal dealt with that que s tion: "Lastly, it was argued on behalf of the applicant that t he punishment awarded to him is disproportionate to the gravi ty of the charge proved against him and is in stark contrast to the punishment awarded by his other three colleagues in whose cases only future increments were stopped, the maxi mum being for three year in respect oth er Shri SainDitt a. " The Tribunal held that t hat the punishment inflicted was disproportionate to th e gravi sion of the Charge proved against the Respondent and was in star k contrast to punishment awarded f or his other two colleagues in whom only future increment were stopped. It also observed that the respondent w as not only master mind to commit the fraudulent act a nd there were others too, and as such he should not be mea s ured with a different yardstick. The question which has to be decided is whether the Tribunal has power to modify the penalty award ed to the Respondent when the findings recorded as to h is misdemeanour is supported by legal evidence. Jurisdiction, powers and authority of t he Central Administrative Tribunal: 27 (1) Save as otherwise expressly provided in this Act, the Central Administrative Tribu nal shall exercise on and from the appointed day all the jurisdiction, powers a nd authority exercisable immediately before that day by a courts (except Supreme Court) in relation to: (a) recruitment, and matters concerningommod i tions,ruitment, to any All India Service or to any civil service of the Union or a Civil post under the Unionor to a po st connected with defence or in the defence services, being in either case, a post filled by a civilian; The Act thus excludes the jurisdiction power, power and a u thority of all Courts except the Supreme Court and confe rs the same on the Tribunal in relation t ing to recruitment a nd service matters. 14, 15, 16, 27, 28 and 29, it becomes apparent that in the case of proceedings transferr ed to tho Tribunal from a civil court or High Court, the Tribu al has the jurisdiction to exercise all the powers whi ch the Civil Court could in a suit or the High Court in a proceeding could have respectively exercised. Because, the Tribunal is just a substitute to t he civil court and High Court. Mah a jan, learned counsel for the Central Government urged th at the Tribunal had no power to interfere with the punishme nt imposed by the disciplinary authority on the ground that it is disproportionate lo the proved misdemeanour. It will be open to Govern ment to decide whether, on the basis of the charges, the punishment of dismissal should be maintain ed 'or else whether a lesser punishment would suffice.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff in a suit for declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property known as 'Palmar Oiteral do Predio Aivao ' comprising seven lots of coconut grove situated at Caranzalem belonging to defendant No. 2. The said suit was dismissed on Match 28, 1974 on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit under section 7 read with section 58(2) of the Bombay Tenancy Act, 1948 could not lie. On appeal, the High Court held that the subject matter of the second suit was directly and substantially in issue in the previous suit between the same parties and hence regardless of the relief claimed the second plaintiff suit was clearly barred by res judicata. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that even though his lease was not terminated as provided by section 9 of the Act, defendant No 1 had dispossessed him by an act of trespass. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1.1 The question whether a person is a tenant or a deemed tenant was required to be decided by the Mamlatdar and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court stood ousted by section 58 (2) specifically bars the jurisdiction from settling, deciding, deciding or dealing with any question which is by or under the Act required to he settled, decided or dealt with by the Tahsildar. [1024C] 1.2 In the instant case, the plaintiff came to court contending that even if his lease had been terminated as stipulated by section 18 of the Tenancy Act the defendant No1 had dispossessed the plaintiff by an order of trespass and therefore, he sought the Court 's assistance to protect his possession by a prohibitory injunction. When in the course of that suit it was found that the defendant had in fact been dispossessed, there was no question of granting an injunction and the only relief which the court could have granted was in regard to the declaration sought which the Court held could not be granted in view of the provisions of Specific Relief Act. [1124D E] 1:3 The impact of the Fifth Amendment may give rise to a situation where the remedy lies entirely under the statute and may have to be taken in the manner prescribed by orunder the Act. For example, where a person who is deemed tenant under section 4 of the Maharashtra Tenancy Act if evicted from the land on or after 1st July 1962 his remedy under section 8(2), is to approach the authority under the Bombay Act for recovery of possession of land of which he has been dispossessed. In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemedtenant whose case is not governed by section 8 (2). But in the instant ease, the defendant plaintiff came into court contending, that even although his lease period was not termination as provided under section 9, he had dispossessed it by an Act of trespass, and therefore the question which arose in the suit was whether defendant No I was a tenant in respect of the lands in question. [1225E F] 1 :4 The impact or the Fifth amendment may give way to a problem where the remedies lies entirely within the Act and may also have to he taken in such manner prescribed under or under that Act. In the present case, it would be for the trial court to determine the course to be adopted in the light of the guidelines indicated hereinabove. [1325E] 2.5 The impact and effect of the Sixth Amendment may given rise to an situation where a remedy lies totally under the provisions Act and there is no express saving clause permitting the Civil court to decide the same, it is obvious that any decision rendered by the Civil Courts would be without jurisdiction.

The petitioners are carpenters 1st and 2 grade employed at the Wood Working Centre of Himachal Pradesh State Handicrafts Corporation (the "Corpo ration"). They are termed as daily rated employees. In this petition under Article 32 of the Constitution they are seeking enforcement of their fundamental right to have equal pay for equal work. They demand payment in terms paid to their counterparts in regular services. They want the same pay of the regular employees as carpenter or in the alternative, the minimum wages prescribed by the Deputy Commissioner for like categories of workmen. They also sought regularisation of their services with the benefits of pen sion, gratuity etc. The Corporation resisted the petitioners ' claim. The case of the Corporation is that the unit where the petition ers are working is a factory registered under the Factories Act and the main object of the Corpora tion as seen from the Memorandum of Association is to preserve the traditional arts and crafts and also to popularise handicrafts and handloom items in the State of Himachal pradesh and other parts of the country and abroad. In order to achieve this primary objec tive, the Corporation gives training to artisans, weavers and craftmen in various traditional arts & crafts. During the period of training, the trainees are paid a stipend by the Corporation. Upto 31st March 1987, the Corporatio n has imparted training to as many as 1662 persons in different areas like carpet weaving, handloom, painting, metal crafts, wood carving, etc. Apart from giving training, The Corpora t tion also ensures marketing support to the artisans and crarafts by purchasing their products at remunerative prices and sell them through the marketing network of the corporation. It is thus a service oriented organisation helping the village artisans & cragesmen to produce and market their products on remuneratory prices. It has suffered huge loss and the total losses accumulated hitherto is Rs.69.77 lakhs. However, for the purpose of preserv ing and promoting traditional arts, craftsmen in different traditional arts or crafts the Corporat ion has been kept alive. But to avoid or minimise further loss, it is stated that the Corporation has reduced its overheads and maintained only the administrative staff in the production centers at different parts of tho State and no permanent craftsman are employed. With these facts, the Court may turn to the principle upon which the petitioners case is rested. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" is not one of the fundamental rights expressly guaranteed by our Constitution. The princi ple was incorporated only under Article 39(d) of the Consti tution as a Directive Principle of State Policy. Perhaps, forthe first time, this Court in Randhir Singh vs Union of India, ; has innovated that it is a constitu tional goal capable of being achieved through constitutional remedies. There the Court pointed out that principle has to be read into Article 14 of the Constitu tion which enjoins the State not to deny any person equality before the law or the equal protection of the law and also To Article 16 which declares that there should be equality of opportu nity for all citizens in matters relating to employment or appointment to any office under the State. The Court pointed Out that principle had to be interpreted into Article14 of the Con stitution as a directive Principle of state Policy. It was also held that it was open to the State to classify employees on the basis of qualifications, duties and responsibilities of the posts concerned. If the classification has reasonable nexus with the objective sought to be achieved, efficiency in the administration, the State would be justified in prescribing different pay scales.

The prosecution alleged that the accused entered into a criminal conspiracy to commit murders of young girls and women in the vicinity of Babultara village by inflicting injuries on the private parts of the victims or disfiguring their faces in order to make it appear that the said seven accused and the approver P.W. 1 were not the real culprits and that in pursuance of that conspiracy they committed the murder of one Malan on or about 29th November 1975. The Sessions Judge found that on a consideration of the evidence, all the seven accused not guilty of the charge of conspiracy framed under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and acquitted them. He found accused 1 to 3 not guilty but accused 1 and 6 guilty of charge No. 2 framed against them in respect of the murder. The High Court dismissed the appeal of accused 5 and convicted him of all the charges framed against him. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the State that (1) the conviction of accused 1 alone for conspiracy under section 120B I. P.C., is unsustainable in law as at least two persons are required for an offence of conspiracy under Section 120A I.p.C.; and (2) the evidence regarding recovery of blood stained razor, article 54 and the medical evidence of Dr. Suresh (P.W 31) who had conducted autopsy on the body of Malan at 4.15 p.m. on 2nd January 1976 was not reliable and that the Sessions Judge acted also upon the retracted judicial confession of accused No. 5 in holding that the guilt of accused 6 for the murder was proved beyond all reasonable doubt. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The retracted judicial confessions of accused5 could not be relied upon against accused 6 in view of the fact that accused 6 who had been tried alongwith accused 5 had been acquitted by the High Court of the charges of conspiracy. [785C] 2. The evidence regarding the presence of accused 785 6 along with accused 7 and P,W.1 near about the scene of offence before and after the commission of the crime of Malinan was amply corroborated by other evidence and it acted also on the retractedjudicial confession of Accused 5 in respect thereof. [781D] 3. The conviction of one of the accused alone for the offence of murder of Malnan under section302 read with Section 34 I P. C. is unsustainable, in law having regard to the requirement of s.120A I P .C. [784E F] 4. The prosecution has failed to prove beyond reasonable doubt that accused 1 had conspired with the seven other accused to commit these three murders or contend that in view Of that circumstance and the finding of the High court that the approver 'P. W. 1 also was a party to the conspiracy the conviction could be sustained. [783E] 5. The medical evidence regarding incised wounds on various parts of body of the Malan was fully corroborated by the other evidence, namely, recovery of the blood stained clothes and razors, article 55 54 and medical evidence. The doctor found 9 incised wounds caused on various part of the body including the right side of the parietal eminance were caused by hard and blunt objects, that death must have been instantaneous and that injuries 1 to 7 collectively were sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [779G H] 6.

The appellant, who was the sole executor of a will alleged to have been executed by one Lakshmamma on August 22, 1945, (exhibit A) in favour of his wife and son, filed a suit for declaration that the said properties were the last testament of Lakshmma. The trial court held that the will was genuine and valid to the extent of the share belonging to the testatrix. On appeal by the appellant, the High Court held that it had not been proved that when Lakshmabai was alleged to had executed the will she was in a sound disposing state of mind or that it was her will in the sense that it represented her intentions. It further held that even if it had found in favour Of the appellant on these two points it would not have been of any help to him because his case must inevitably fail when it is held that he had really understood its contents, had approved of them and had put her signatures on it when she was ill at Mandya. On this finding the High court came to the conclusion that the appellant had failed to prove that the money for the purchase of items 3, 4 and 5 came out of any bequest under Annaji 's will (ex exhibit A) and so in its opinion Lakshmamamma could not claim any share in the said property. The High Court also held that there was no evidence in rebuttal led by respondent 1. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the onus of proving execution of the will had been shifted on the propounder to remove the suspicions attending the execution of a document and to establish that Lakshmama had really known its contents. Held: (i) The High court was in error in coming to the conclu sion that it Was not shown that the testatrix fully understood the contents of the Will and put her signature on it, when she attested the will. (ii) The onus of establishing execution of an instrument lies heavily upon the propounder who sets up a strong case for the application of any principle or rule of law which is applicable to all cases. It may be stated generally that a propounder of the testator 's mind and his signature as required by law, courts would be justified in making a finding in favour o the propounder. (iii) The burden of proving the execution lies heavily on the party who sets it up on the onus. In the present case there was nothing to show that the propounder fully understood or the contents thereof. The evidence of Kalbagal that he knew nothing about the execution was read over to the executant so as to enable her to understand its full effect before it was signed by his. (iv) The appellant obtained a power of attorney from the testatrix on the same day and had given rise to the argument that the appel lant was keen on taking possession and management of the properties under his control even before the death of the testatrix, could not be accepted. (v) The evidence showed that the executant knew nothing of the execution or of the deed until the appellant asked him to get some attesting witnesses for the will, and this evidence did not strike as natural or probable; but apart from it, even Kalbagmal 's evidence does not show satisfactorily that the Will was read out to the propounder so as not to enable the appellant to understand their full effect.

The appellant company manufactured Arcons, known as "Cinema Arc Carbons" manufactured by it. The use to which they were generally put, showed that the common or ordinary use of the arc carbons was that they exuded their power foul light cast through the projectors, on cinema screens. It was pointed out that the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal under the Act had allowed an application for adducing expert evidence to determine the question whether are carbon manufactured by the appellant company could be covered by the entry under consideration. The High Court held that these were carbers falling within Entry 41 of Schedule 1 of the Madras General Sales Tax Act, 1957 and dismissed the appeal without taking further evidence. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods under consideration are covered by Entry No. 4 of the 1st Schedule to the Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: The term "accessories" is used in the schedule to describe goods which may have been manufactured for use as an aid or addition. A sense in which the word accessory is used is given in Webster 's Third New International Dictionary as follows: "all objects or device that is not essential in itself but that adds to the beauty, convenience or effectiveness of something else". [564B] The Andhra Pradesh High Court correctly held that the main use of tile arc car bons under consideration was duly proved to be that of production of powerful light used in projectors in cinemas. The fact that they can also be used for search lights, signalling stage lighting, or where powerful lighting for photography or other purposes may be required, could not detract from the classification to which the carbon arcs belong. That is determined by their ordinary or commonly known purpose or user. This, as already observed by this Court, is evident from the fact that the appellants are known as 'cinema arc carons ' in the market. This finding was enough, in our opinion, to justify the view taken by the Andhra PradeshHigh Court that the primary use of these were Carbons under the consideration was properly proved to he that of the production of suitable match light used In projectors or other cinematographic equipment.

The petitioners in these petitions challenged the validity of a notification issued by the Government of Gujarat on June 26, 1985 amending the Gujarat Minor Mineral Rules 1966. The petitioners contended that the royalty levied and covered under the rules should be applied only for mineral development and since the said royalty is being treated as part of the consolidated fund of the State and used for other purposes by the State the levy was bad; and 2. that the impugned notification in question was in contravention of clause (b) of Article 304 of the Constitution. The respondents contended that under Entry 50 of List II of the 7th Schedule to the Constitution, the royalty recovered by the Govern ment forms part of consolidated fund and the said tax can be used only for minerals specified in column 2 of the schedule. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Act is passed for devel opment of minerals, but while discharging its functions relating to development, if the State incidentally allows mining to be carried on in public interest and levies in that connection a tax, it does not mean that the said taxes should be used merely for development of minerals and not for other pur poses sanctioned by law. The minerals belong to the Government and if anybody wants to have the right as a lessee to exploit the mines in question to the exclusion of all others and to remove the minerals with a view to making profit, he has to pay a royalty imposed in accordance with law. [439C D] 1.2 In the instant case, the petitioners are lessees who are exploiting the mining areas for purposes of business and that the royalties in question belong to them. Under clause 1 of the proviso to the impugned rule 21, a holder of a Parwana granted under the Rules has to Pay royalty at the rate of 50 per cent of the royalty payable by the lessees and no royalty is payable by village potters who manufacture upto one lakh bricks per year and by the village potter whose annual production was not exceeding two lakh bricks and who supply at least one lakh brick bricks to the Rural Housing Board or Panchayats. His contention was that section 15 of the Act which authorised the State Government to make rules in respect of minor minerals does not specifically authorise the State Govern ment to make such discrimination. It is well settled that a classification to be valid has to satisfy two conditions: (1) that there is an intelligible differentia between those who are included in the class which is affected by any law or rule and those who arc placed outside the said rule; and (2) that it is equally clear that while levying a tax the authority con cerned is entitled to grant concessions and exemptions wherever necessary having regard to the purpose of the statute, the levy of royalty is incidental to the regulation and development of mineral. It was only in the case of such people who are described in the Rules and who invariably belong to weaker sections of society the concession is shown under rule 21 whereas the mining lease may be given to persons mentioned in rule 9.

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Mudaliars of Manjakollai village. According to the appellant, the temple was rounded two hundred years ago by the members of his community and since then the management of the temple and is affairs was always vested in the community of the Sangunatha Mudaliar Community and no person other than the elected trustee had at any time the right of management and control of the Temple. The respondents took a different view and proceeded on the basis that trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The Subordinate Judge held that the appellant 's suit was barred by limitation. On appeal, the High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the judgment of the Subordinate Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the succession was "regulated by usage" and that according to the usage of the deity the trustees were elected for a period of one year each at a meeting of the members ' of the Sangunatha Ammal Community and so the appellant must be held to be a trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of Act 19 of 1951. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The word "succession" in relation to property and rights and interests in property generally implies "passing of an interest from one person to another". [445 B] State of Madras vs Ramakrishna, ; , followed. (2) It is not possible to say that there is a succession of As office to another when on the efflux of the period for which A was appointed, there is vacancy and B is elected to that vacancy. It is quite possible that for that vacancy A himself might be reelected because a retiring trustee is eligible for reelection. The possibility of A being the successor A himself is not merely an anomaly, it is an impossible legal position. No man can succeed to his own office. In Black 's Law Dictionary the word "Succession ' is defined as follows: "The revolution of title to property under the law of descent and distribution. (1 ) The right by which one set of men may, by succeeding another set, acquire a property in all the goods, movables, and other chattels of a corporation." [446 C] State vs Ramakrishna; , referred to.

The appellant was the village Munsif. On April 26, 1971 at about 10 P.M. he was sleeping on a bench outside his cattle shed in the open space, which is shown in the site plan (exhibit P15). Pandurangam woke up at about 11.15 P.m. He got up and saw the accused Karunakaran running ahead of accused Karunakarhan. He also saw his two brothers, Gnanasakaran (PW 1) and Thiru gnanasambandam (PW 3) chasing them. He ran to his elder brother who came from the side of the bench where he was sitting and fell down on the northern side of a sluice. When he went near him he was already dead. He had bleeding injuries on several parts of his body. A crowd gathered and Pandurangam was asked to lodge information at the police station which he did. The doctor (PW 16) who held the postmortem examination found nine injuries two of which he described as incised and four as punctured, two more incised wounds and one more incised wound. These were on the left side of his back. The deceased succumbed to the injuries on various parts of the body. The appellant was convicted under section 302 IPC and sentenced to death. On appeal by the State, the High Court acquitted him. In this appeal by special leave it was contended that (1) there had been a history of a bitter feud spanning over nearly a decade between the first accused and his father on the one hand and the deceased Viswanatham t on the other; (2) the High court erred in convicting the appellant on the sole testimony of PW 4, "corroborated by the contents of exhibit P1 (FIR). HELD: 1. The High Court was not even right that PW 4 stands wholly corroborated by the content of the FIR. On the other hand it has made a correct approach in assessing the quality of the evidence of this solitary eye witness. [712 F] 2. There is considerable doubt as to this testimony with regard to seeing the accused running away from the place where he is sleeping to the place when he fell dead. The fact that this eye witness could be persuaded to substitute PWs 1, 2 and 3 for his deceased brother as chasing the assailants, degrades him from the status of an absolutely reliable witness. He is definitely an obliging witness and cannot at all be trustworthy. This witness may not have a qualm of conscience in implicating the accused for the mere asking by someone, if not by the inimical police officer (PW 23) against whom criminal cases were pending at the instance of the accused 's father.

The respondents were partners in a firm of solicitors. Amarchand N. Shroff, Mangaldas and Hiralal up to November 30, 1949, and on December 1, 1949 Ramesh son of Amarchand who had by then qualified as a solicitor joined the firm as the third partner. For the assessment years 1950 51 and 1951 52 he assessed the amounts in the hands of the heirs and legal representatives of Amar Chand N. The matter was not pursued further by the Revenue but sometime later proceedings were started by the Income tax Officer under section 34 in respect of the same income in the hand of " Amarchand ' N. It was contended on behalf of the Commissioner of Income tax that on a correct interpretation of section 24B the amounts which were received by the heirs, legal representatives and just as the deceased Amarchand after his death should be deemed by the fiction incorporated in sub section (1) to be income received by Amarchand and liable to tax under section 24 B(1) of the Income Tax Act. Held, that on the facts and circumstances of the case the sums of Rs. 32,523/ were not assessable to income tax under s.24B as his income in their hands was liable to be assessed to income 'tax under section 23B(1), but in that case also the amount was received by him after his heirs and the legal representatives after his demise but in the previous year and it was earned by the deceased during the previous years. The fiction is limited to the cases provided in the three subsections of section24B and cannot be extended beyond the object for which it was enacted. Commissioner of Incometax, Bombay City vs The State of Bihar, ; , referred to.

The petitioners were employed in the ministerial services of the Andhra Pradesh Government. All of them were working in various offices located in the cities of Hyderabad and Secunderabad. On January 19, 1969, leaders of political parties in the Legislature of the State appeared to have met and reached the decision that to Implement what are called Telengana area ', the following measures should be taken : "All non domicile persons who have been appointed either directly by promotion or by transfer to posts reserved under the Andhra pradesh Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Rules, 1959 for domiciles of Telengna region will be immediately relieved from service. The posts so rendered vacant will be filled by qualified candidates possessing domicile qualifications and in cases where such candidates are not available the posts shall be left unfilled till qualified domicile candidates become available. Action on these lines will be taken immediately. All non domicile employees so relieved shall be provided employment in the Andhra region without break in service and by creating supernumerary posts, if necessary. " The action was based upon section 3 of the Public Employment(Requiresment as To Residence) Act, 1957, which was an Act of Parliament made in pursuance of cl. (3) of article 16 of the Constitution making special provision for requirement as to residence and brought into force on March 21, 1959. Section 3 gave the power to make rules prescribing, in regard to appointments to (a) any subordinate service or post under the State Government of Andhra Pradesh, or any requirement as regards residence within that State or Union territory prior to such appointment; (b) any requirement, as to resident within that state, the present words from 'under the Government ' to 'Union territory ' have been substituted. The petitioners challenged the Act and the Rules on the ground that article 16(3) was not ultra vires the Constitution. Held: (i) Article 16(1) of the Constitu tion is a special provision and comes as an amendment must dictate that a narrow construction upon the exception should be placed as indeed the debates in the Constituent Assembly also seem to indicate. The word 'State ' here is to be understood in the extended meaning given to it by the definition of that word. The unit State is only meant and not any part thereof. It follows, therefore, that section 3 must be read narrowly and not carried to excess by interpretation. The Article speaks of residence within a State and means only that if it chose to speak of residence in parts of State such as Districts, talauqas, cities towns etc. more appropriate and specific language could have been used such as 'any requirement asto residence within the State or union territory prior thereto '. (ii) The word State ' here was not to be interpreted narrowly but must be understood not carried with excess by construction. The words 'residence within the meaning of article 35(b) in so far as it relates to Telengaana (and we say nothing about the other parts) and Rule 3 of Rules under it are ultra vires.

The appellant was tried for offences under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898. The prosecution case was that when the house in which the appellant lives along with his father and had a key with him it must be he who must be deemed to be in possession of the almirah and consequently of its contents including the registered letters in question. The High Court held that the appellant had secreted the five registered letters and on this finding set aside his acquittal and convicted him in each of the three appeals for offences tinder section 52 Of the Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a period of one year in each case. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (1) the prosecution having merely shown that the registered letter were recovered from an almirah in the house, the key of which was produced by the appellant 's father could not sustain an inference that the almirah contained apart from the registered documents in question, certain other articles belonging to the appellant cannot sustain an presumption that the depositor was in possession exclusively or jointly with his mother; (2) the mere fact that there is even a delay of several months in delivering a postal article to the addressee would not mean that the article had ceased to be In course of transmission. Held:(i) The prosecution has failed to prove that these letters were in the exclusive possession of appellant. No presumption can, therefore, be drawn against him that he had secreed them from the mere mere fact of possession, according to the High Court itself, is a speculative reason and must, therefore be left out of consideration. (ii) The evidence adduced by the prosecution was not sufficient to establish that these were in his exclusive possession along with the appellant.

The appellants were convicted of contempt of court and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 1,000/ and further ordered that in case of default they shall undergo simple imprisonment for two weeks. The High Court held that the five appellants had disobeyed an order of stay passed by it staying proceedings pending before the Nyaya Panchayat. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Magistrate had no jurisdiction to stay proceedings pending receipt of the stay order; (2) the Nyaya Panchayats acted in a judicial capacity and therefore the Magistrate committed contempt of the court; and (3) the High Court erred in not relying on the fact that the High 's stay order was stayed by the High Courts. HELD : (i) The High Courts were right in holding that the Nyaya panchayats exercised judicial powers and even if the Panchas erred in staying proceedings, before finding them guilty of contempt, it should be definitely proved that the order was passed deliberately to pass the order of the High court. [119 E] (ii) In the present case the High .Court did not appreciate that the so called affidavit which was filed before the Panchas was in fact not an affidavit at all. It had not been sworn to before any person authorised to administer oaths. It was no part of the duty of the Pan chachas to enquire from the S.D.M about the filing of the application before him. At any rate, he has apparently no jurisdiction in his discretion adjourn proceedings, it cannot be said that he had committed contempt. [120 F G] (iii) The so called affidavits which were filed before a Magistrate was in substance not an affidavits at all and it had not . been sworn before any persons authorised to do so. It is no part Of the duty to enquire into from the person who has knowledge of the existence of the order. At that rate, the Sarpanch had apparently no jurisdic tion to stay proceeding before the Magistrate when no Proceeding was pending before him, and it was not necessary that the Magistrate should have asked the applicant to produce a certified copy of the stayed order.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge, Etawah under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death. The High Court did not rely on this extra judicial confession. It relied on certain statements made by the appellant in his report dictated at the Police Station and considered those facts together with the motive and the evidence about the purchase of the sword sufficient to confirm the appellant 's conviction and sentence. The Sessions Judge believed that the appellant had murdered Sheo Sahai, but did not tell him the reason. The appellant adduced no evidence in support of his statement. The evidence led by the prosecution consisted of the evidence relating to motive, to his extrajudicial confession to one Ujagar Singh when he was having a bath in the Canal at that hour and by Bishram Singh, P.W. 13, who 210 deposed that Ujagar Singh stated that he had come after committing the murder of Sheo Sahai and asked him what. led him to have a bath at that time at night. The extra judicial confessions were not usually considered with favour but that does not mean that such a confession coming from a person who has no reason to state falsely and to whom it is made in circumstances which tend to support his statement, should not be believed. The murder was committed in the month of June. Both on account of the temperature and on account Of the culprit 's desire to wash of blood marks on his person, the appellant his bathing in the canal at that hours of the night cannot be said to be improbable. It is not therefore a matter of surprise that he wakes up and proceeds to the spot from where the splashing sound which, is supposed to be due to the wading of the neel gais came. On reaching the Canal bank he observes 209 the person bathing and naturally asks him what led him, to have A bath at the said hour at night and byjhram Singh. The Canal runs beside Ujagar Singh 's field. Ujagar Singh went to the village at about 5 a.m., and they told the people of what he had been told by the appel lant. This statement of his was supported by Paley Singh, who states that the Sub Inspector was not present when Ujagar Singh related to them the fact which had taken place at night, and byJugram Singh the appellant thought the best thing to be to proceed to the Police station and report about it. The letter written by the Sub inspector to the police officer was also signed by him. The confession of the appellant to Ujagar Singh was not recorded in his presence. The statement of the SubInspector was not admissible in evidence as it amounted to a confession of an offence by the accused made to a Police Officer and that he did commit the murder. The trial court accepted the prosecution case against the appellant and convicted him under section 201 I. P.C. and sentenced him to death, but the High Court dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellent that the entire report dictated by the appellants was inadmissible in evidence because its contents amounted to confession of a offence by an accused made before a Police officer and that the extra judicial confessional confession together with other circumstances relied upon by the High court were insufficient to establish conclusively that the person who possessed it so shortly after the murder had committed the murder, and that such portions of the report which did not amount to a direct admission of the appellants striking Sheo Sahai with a sword and thereby causing his death were admissible in Evidence. Held: (i) The extrajudicial confessions made by an appellant to a police officer are not usually consider with favour, but that do not mean, that such confession coming into from a persons who hasno reason to say falsely and which it is make in circumstances tend to supporting his statement should not he believed.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Raipur published the preliminary electoral roll on September 30, 1978 under Rule 4(1) of the Madhya Pradesh Munici pal Corporation (Preparation, Revision and Publication of Electoral Rolls and Selection of Councillors) Rules 1963. The Collector published the final electoral roll under Rule 8 of the Rules on November 16, 1978 notifying that the poll, if necessary, would take place on December 31, 1978 in all the 44 constituencies: Six petitioners including the appellants presented a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on December 28, 1978 requesting the court to make an order quashing the electoral roll and the calendar of events issued for the purpose of the said election and directing the respondents not to notify the results of the election under Rule 46 of the rules pending disposal of the petition. The writ petition itself was filed on December 29, 1978 when the poll had to take place in all 44 constituencies; six petitioners including appellants presented their claim and that the applications were disposed of on October 30,1978. The Deputy Collector rejected the claims and objections made by the appellants. Thereafter the successful candidates were also impleaded as respondents and the petition was amended by inclusion of an additional prayer that the declaration of results of all the 43 successful candidates should also be quashed. After the respondents filed their counter affidavits, the petition being heard and it was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High court on January 20, 1979. The appellants thereupon filed a writ petition in the High Courts challenging the validity of the electoral rolls and the declaration thereof of results. The learned Single Judge before whom the case came up for orders directed the issue of notice of the petitions and the stay application to the respondents and issued an interim order directing the respondent not to publish the results. On December 31. 1978, the poll was held and 44 persons were declared elected. Their names were, however, not published under Rule 56 of the Munichi pal Corporation Rules in view of the interim order made by this Court. Thereafter, the successful candidate were also included as respondents. The petition was filed in December 1979 for a writ of certiorari quashing the election proceedings on the ground that the entire election process had become vitiated on account of the defect in the notice issued under Rule (1) Of the Rules notifying that claims and objection should be preferred within 30 days from the date of publication of that notice when sub rule (3) of Rule 4 of the Act prescribed that such claims and/or objections could be preferred. The Division Bench dismissed the writ petition on January 21, 1979 holding that the petitioners were not prompt in moving the High courts after undue delay. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The final electoral rolls were published on November 25, 1978 and it is only on December 5, 1978 for the first time that a letter was addressed by petitioner No. 6 to the Collector drawing his attention to the error that had crept into the notice published under rule 4(i) of Rules. The final list of candidates for the election with their symbols was published on December 20, 1978.

The first respondent company, its directors and the second respondent, its Directors for failure to Me with the Registrar of Companies on or before 30 10 1967 the balance sheet and profit and loss account of the company as required under section 220(1) of the , which is punishable under sub section (3) of that section. The appellants were prosecuted under sections 32(5) and 133(3) read with section 220 of the Companies Act, 1913 for failure of Me to Me. The first respondent filed a complaint against the appellants on or about 30 10 67 1967 alleging that the balance sheets and profit loss account had not been laid before a general body meeting nor could it be so laid. The High Court dismissed the complaint holding that if no balance sheet was laid before the general body, there can be no question of that balance sheet not being adopted nor of complying with the requirements of section 220 and though wilful omission to call a general Body meeting and to lay the balancesheet and profit account before it may expose the person responsible to punishment under other provisions of the Act, it certainly does not make him liable under the provisions of section 134(4) of Companies Act. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (1) The holding of the annual general meeting and the laying before it of the balance Sheet and profit or loss account is a sine qua non for filing of the copies thereof before the Registrar. [416 E] (2) The finding that section 26 makes the offence a continuing one also shows that the obligation to file the list is independent of the holding of a general meeting. It is clear therefore that on principle and authority it should be held that no offence was committed by the directors in this case under section 134. They might have been guilty of offences under sections 76 and 133 but not under section134. [417 F] (3)(a) The contention that provisions (1), (2), (3), (4) and (5) show that the failure to file a list is an independent of holding of general meeting was accepted. But under section 26(2) of 1913 Act, the obligation of sending three copies of the Balance sheet and profits and loss accounts or the income and expenditure account as the case may be, arises only after they have been laid for before the company at the general meeting three copies thereof shall be filed with the registrar, and a failure to do so is made penal by the Act. [414 G] (b) The provisions of sections 134 and 220 show that on principles and authority they should be found guilty of offence under section 135. They may have been convicted for offences under section 76 and 132 but not otherwise. [413 F] In the present case, the holding was of the general meetings and the lay before it at the meeting three copy copies thereof were filed with Registrar and the failure of to reach any one of the stages within the time prescribed is made punishable by the 'Act. The liability of sending 3 copies of balance sheet or profit and losses account or the Income and expenditure accounts, as the ease may be. arises only when they have already been laid after the company has been placed before the Company at a general Meeting. It was not open to the appellants to plead in answer to a charge under sections 134 their prior default in respect of the calling of the prescribed general meeting, and that the company and its directors could not rely upon their failure to call the general Body meet as a defence to the prosecution. [409 G H] (4)(a). The finding of the High Court that section 25 makes the offences a continuing offence also shows the obligation on the part of the directors to file them before the ' Registrar.

The respondent was convicted by the Special Court under section 3 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1949, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for two years. The High Court held that though the need for a speedier trial than what is possible under the procedure prescribed by the Code of Criminal Procedure might form the basis of a reasonable classification and section 5(1) could not be regarded as discriminatory in so far as it purported to vest in the State Government an absolute and arbitrary power to refer to a special court for trial "any cases ", which must include an individual case, "whether the duration of such a case is likely to be long or not ". The respondent appealed to this Court. Held: (i) that section 5 of the Act was valid as it did not by its own force make the special procedure provided in the Act applicable to the trial of any offence or classes of cases; for, it was the State Govern ment 's notification under the section that attracts the application of the procedure. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and is not directed towards the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of offences or classes thereof. (ii) that the classification implied was in this sense that judges were to deter mine what is for the good of the people and substitute their individual and personal opinions for that of the government of the day, or that they may usurp the functions of the legislature.

The appellant was a Radiologist in the Maulana Azad Medical College. He was appointed as an Associate Professor of Radiotherapy in the year 1964. The post of Radiologist cum Associate Professor was later redesignated as Assistant Professor of radiotherapy. On October 9, 1964, he was promoted to the post of Associate Professor. After completing his academic years in the grade of Associate Professors, he filed a return reiterating the stand taken by the Government of India in the Health Ministry that the appellant could not be considered for appointment to the said post. The appellant contended that the qualifications prescribed for teaching post the teaching experience gained by him while holding the post were of Radiological cum Associate Professors and Assistant Professors in the Medical Colleges and that he was not eligible for appointment as Professor or Radiology in Maulana Gandhi Medical College because the teaching work done by him was a teaching post. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that since the appellant had the essential qualification prescribed for the teaching post, his appointment could not he taken into consideration for the purpose of determining the question of his eligibility for appointment. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The qualifications prescribed in Annexure I to the Second Schedule are the same as those prescribed by the Central Health Service (Amendment) Rules 1966. [27D] 2.1 The appellant who admittedly is a highly qualified person and has the requisite teaching experience as Radiologistcum Associate Professor in the Hospital cannot be appointed by direct recruitment as Professor of Pathotherapy under r. (2). That being so, the appellant who undoubtedly is a high qualified person, and has requisite teaching training as Radiology cum Associate professor of Radiography (ex officio) is clearly eligible for appoint ment as Professor/ Radiotherap in Ma Gurudwara Medical College which had fallen vacant in 1973. [28E F] 2:2 The post in question is a post belonging to the Specialists Grade II carrying a pay scale of Rs. 8 (3) provides that 50% of the vacancies in Supertime Grade II to be filled by promotion of General Duty Officers Grade I and Specialists ' Grade Officers in the ratio of 2 : 3 on the basis of merit and seniority and the remaining 50% Of the vacancies are to be carried by direct recruit in the manner specified in the Second schedule. That is to say, there is certain amount of flexibility and it cannot be that the Appellant who is a Radiologycum Associate professor in the Willing don Hospital or the Safdarjang Hospital and the mere designation of the appellant as such does not give him a right to hold the post Of Professor of pathological Surgery in Ma Guru Gurudwaras Medical College, New Delhi. By parity of reasoning, it is urged that the designation of appellant as a Radiographer cum Associate Assistant Professor in Radiotheology (executive) did not make him eligible for promotion to the Post of Associate professor or Radiologist In Maulana Safdar Medical College and the Mere designation of his appellant as an Assistant Professor does not confer upon him a Right to hold a post of Professor of Automorology in the Gurudwar Medical College for the post graduate and under graduate students of the Ma Gurindwara Medical college. [29H; 30A] 2 :3 The appellant was not only holding the Post but was also actively associated with teaching the under graduate and post graduate students as an assistant Professor of Surotherapy (ex officio) in the Irwin Hospital, which is a teaching hospital attached to the Ma ul Azad Medical college for the M.D., D.M.R.T. and M.B.S. courses of studies for the last 17 years.

The workmen of Orient Paper Mills Ltd., Brajrajnagar, have come up in this appeal by special leave against an award of the Industrial Tribunal, Orissa. An industrial dispute between these workmen and the management of Orient paper Mills Ltd. (the Company) was referred by the State Government under section 10(1)(d) of the , for adjudication by the Tribunal enumerating 30 different items of dispute. Ltd., Dwarka Cement Works, Dwarka vs Its Workmen and Another ; , referred to. HELD : The Tribunal committed no error of fact requiring interference by this court in basing its decision on the principle contained in the earlier Agreement of 1959. [466 F] French Motor car Co. (1), Hirakud; and Aluminjure Company Ltd., ; , applied. French Motor Co. vs Its workmen, ; , followed. French motor Car Co., Ltd. Dwarka Cement 's Works, ; and French Motor Company Co. v Its Workmen, [1963] Supp. 1 S.C.R.

The assessee, a partnership firm, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1960 61. The notice issued under section 148 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1961, stated that the assessee had reason to believe that his income chargeable to tax for that year had escaped assessment within the meaning of section 147 of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee also produced before him a statement showing various creditors from whom it borrowed on Hundis during the accounting year in question. In that statement it gave the lull names and address of the alleged creditors. After enquiry, the assessee 's total income was assessed at Rs. 69,886/ . On June 3, 1966, the 1st respondent issued to the assessee a notice under section 147(a) of the Act. The material portion of that notice reads as follows "Notice under section 149 of the I.T.O. 30 4 66. Whether it is a new case or one in which re assessment (or recomputation) has to be made Re assessment 5. If a case of reassessment (or Computation) the income (or loss or depreciation allowance originally assessed/determined. Rs. 73,604/ 6. Whether the case falls under cl. (a) or (b) of section 148 147(A) 7. The Income tax Officer issued to him a notice containing all or any of the requirements which may be included in a notice. The 1st Respondent challenged the validity of that order on various grounds, and as he was accepting the contention of the assessee that the impugned notice was invalid inasmuch as it did not comply with the requirements of section 151(2) of Act, he had no jurisdiction to issue a notice thereunder under section148. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave: HELD : (i) If only he had read the report carefully, he could never have come to the conclusion on the material before him that this is a fit case for the issue of a notice tinder section 148. [447C] (ii) The Commissioner has mechanically accorded permission. He did not himself record that he was satisfied that this was a fit one for the issuance of a fresh notice under s.148.

The appellant was carrying on a business in the past and had been assessed to income tax for the years 1948 49 and 1949 50. The claim was rejected by the Income tax Officer and by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and also by the Incometax Appellate Tribunal on appeal to it. The appellant then moved the Tribunal under section 66(1) of the Act but that application was rejected. The High Court held that the business on which tax had been charged under the Act of 1918 had ceased at any time before 1948 or (b) whether there was a succession by another person for the person who was carrying On April 1, 1939, and therefore, the income from the business could not be said to have been carried on in April 1. Held, that the appellant was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of Income tax Act, 1922, as it had been carrying on business on April 1 but only in respect of the business in piece goods, yarn and banking which alone had paid tax under the Income Tax Act of 1922. The income from business could be said not be a business carried on at the commencement of the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act, 1939. The question whether there is succession was one of the members of the erstwhile family and not by the whole family though I express no opinion upon it but even so that would be a case of succession rather than discontinuance. It was for this reason that sub section (4) Of section 25 expressly mentioned that a case where succession was not to be found where there was mere change in the constitution of the firm, and if so, whether; it amounted to "discontinuance" of business for the application of sub section 4 of section 25.

The appellant 's suit for partition and separate possession of a 7/24th share in two houses, a land, two shops avoid movables on the basis that these properties belonged to the joint family consisting of her husband, herself and their two sons. The plaintiff 's father died in 1960 leaving him surviving his wife Hirabai who is the plaintiff, two sons, and three daughters, defendants 3 to 5. On November 6, 1962 Hirabai filed a special civil suit No. 26 of 1963 in the court of the Joint Civil Judge, Senior Division, Sangli for partition, separate possession and separate Possession of a 8/24 share in the two houses. The trial judge held that the plaintiff became indisputably entitled to a 7 /24th shares and that there was no prior partition and that the appellant was not fully argued and was incorrectly decided and that on a true view of law, the widow 's share must be ascertained by adding the share to which she is entitled at a notional partition during her husband 's life time and the share which she would get in her husband interest upon his death. The High Court dismissed the plaintiff ' 's appeal and allowed the plaintiff respondent 's cross objections by holding that the suit properties belonged only to the Joint family, that there were no prior Partition and that as between them the two sons the three daughters and the widow will take equally, each having one share in it, the other three getting 1/4th share each. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: (1) The High Courts have considered exhaustively the various decisions bearing on the point and we endorse the analysis contained in the judgment of Kantawala C. (1). A Hindu Mitakshara coparcener 's interest in coparcenary property would devolve by survivorship upon the surviving members of the coparcenary and not in accordance with the Act. [766 F] (2) The expression "any property possessed by a female Hindu" is used in section 6(a) of the Hindu Succession Act, 1956. It includes any property acquired before or after the commencement of the Act, but does not include any property which may be acquired under the Act and therefore, it cannot be said that the interest of a Hindu Mitakshara coparcenary can be taken away by an application of the rules of intestate succession contained in sections 8, 9 and 10 of the Indian Succession Act. The proviso to section 6 resorts to the simple expedient, undoubtedly fictional, that the interests of a Mitakshara coparcener "shall be deemed to be" the share in 'the property that would have been allotted to him if a partition of that property had taken place immediately before his death irrespective of whether he was entitled to claim partition or not. [765 H] (3) The assumption having been made once for the purpose of ascertaining the share of the deceased in the coparcenary property, one cannot go back on that assumption and ascertain the share. of the heirs without reference to it. All the consequences which flow from a real partition have to be logically worked out, which means that the share must ascertained on the reasoning that they bad separated from one another and had received a share in that partition which had takenplace during the life time of the testator. [764 A B] (4) The inevitable corollary of this position is that the heir will get his or her share in interest which the deceased bad in the coparcener property at the time of his death, in addition to the share, which he or she received or must be deemed ' to have received in the notional partition. [774 A] (5) The heirs will get their or her shares in the interest which they had received or shall be deemed "to have received" in the actual partition.

The first respondent, a company carrying on life insurance business in India, was compulsorily retired by the Life Insurance Corporation of India (Staff) Regulations 1960. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said regulations and praying for a direction to the appellant Corporation to retire him on completion of 58 years of age. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the employees of the Corpo ration belonging to Class I or Class II were entitled to continue in service till they attained the age of 60 years subject to the usual clause relating to premature retirement. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that since he had the right to continue to work in Class III only till he attained the superannuation age of 58, he could not be reduced to 58 years only because he had been promoted to a class I post or Class 11 post. Allowing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The first Respondent was entitled to retire on completion Of 58 years. [223E] 1.2 The Central Government and the Corporation felt that 60 years of service could be a proper age of retirement in the circumstances in respect of the transferred employees and that was the reason why by regulation 19 and the standardisation order issued earlier in the case of certain classes of transferred em ployees under section 11(2) of the Act, the retirement age was fixed at 60 years and this was done with a view to retaining the services of the experienced employees of tho erstwhile insurers. It was not possible to hold that regulation 19(2), is violative of Article 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [227G H] 1:3 The High Courts erred in striking down Regulation 19(1) as amended in the year 1977, and directing the Corporation to continue the first Respondent in its service till he completed the age Of 60 years. It is true that originally employees belonging to class III and Class IV categories amongst the transferred employ ees were given the benefit of retirement at the ageof 60 years but the employees belong ing to Class III and class IV categories among the transferred employee were given tho benefit of retire ment at the time of superannuation. The employees belonged to Class 111 and ClassIV categories amongst them, who came from companies where there was no rule similar to clause (b) as regards the age or superannuation. Thereafter only one class of employees would be in the service of the Corporation, namely, those appointed subsequent to 1st September 1956 by the Corporation in respect o whom the Corporation has fixed the age for retirement as 58 years which corre sponds to the age age of superannuation in almost all the public sector establishments, the Central Government services and the State Government serv ice. It may be so. [228H; 228A] 2.1 In the instant case, the first respondent was entitled tO continue in his service till the age was 60 years, but the employee belonged to class 111 and class III categories amongst tho transferred employees were given benefit of retired at the ages of 60, but he had not been promoted as on promotion they became persons belonging to the same category of employees enjoying the same conditions of service. It could not therefore be said that Regulation 19 (2) was violative of article 14 and16 of the Constitu tion.

The appellants wrote a letter to the President of India with copies to others with the sole object of conveying the opinion that the public expression by the Hon 'ble Judge of his personal views on controversial matters con cerned the merits and demerits of the present system of Government was not in keeping with the well accepted role of proverbial aloofness of a Judge. The letter stated that Justice D.S. Tewatia of the Punjab and Haryana High Court visited the session division of Bhiwani and inspected the Courts from 14 February 1975 to 19 February 1975. In that letter they also brought to the notice of the President that Justice S.D. Tewar, Bhiwani had visited the courts and inspected them on 17 February 1975 and thereafter stated as follows: "The learned Judge met the members of the Bar on 15 February, 1975 in the Bar Room, Bhiwwani. During the course of his discussion with the members, he discussed politics with them and criticised the present executive in general and the Congress Party in particular. He also enquired all about Shri Sohan Lal a leader of the teacher 's movement in the State". The letter concluded by saying that the Honble Judge during his entire stay in his tour deliberately showed the bent of his mind towards commu nism while exchanging view on various matters. The appellants took a copy of their letter to Chief Justice of Punjab andHaryana High Court, the Chief Minister of Haryana and the Prime Minister. In reply they said that the contents of the letter were not correct. They also stated that the letters written by the appellants were correct. It was intended to be a privileged communication made solely with a view to uphold the dignity of the Court. The deponent has been taught to believe that a Judge ought always to steer clear of all avoidable controversial matter. The High Court did not mention which particular portion of the said letter constituted contempt of court. It is an article of faith with the deponent that dignity and respect of all Courts and of all Judges particularly of the High Court must be maintained for, amongst other reasons on that depends the orderly function ing of the society as also prestige of the profession to which the deponent has the honour to belong. The deponents stated that if the Court is of the view that the letter of the deponents constitute for any reason contempt of Court, no one would be more sorry than the deponent himself. Therefore, the deponent tenders his apology to this Hon ' ble Court for the same and prays for its acceptance." The appellants filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the maintainability of the contempt petition contending that the allegations in the letter amounted to scandalising the Hon`ble Judge or the Court in any manner to weaken people 's faith in the administration of justice. The petition was dismissed by the Full Bench. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that there was no intention whatsoever on his part to scandalise the Hon"ble Judge, or this Hon ble Court or to lower the authority or undermine the prestige of his learned Judge or of the Hon ble court or to weak in any way the confidence of the people in the adminis tration of justice; (2) that the communication did not bear out any foundation for an action for criminal contempt. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1(a) The letter does not interfere much less substantial ly with due course of justice or proper administration of law by the courts. [246E] (b) It will not be correct and proper for any Judge to accept the invitation and hospitality of any busi ness or commercial organisation or of any political party or of a group or organisation run on sectarian, communal or parochial lines.

The petitioner company was a company registered under the Indian Companies Act. Suraj Mall Mohta was also the managing director of another company Messrs. Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. A reference had been made by the Central Government under section 5(1) of the Act before 58 450 1st September, 1948 of the case of Messrs. jute and Gunnny Broking Ltd. to the Investigation Commission appointed under Act XXX of 1947. During the investigation of some other cases similarly referred to the Commission, it was said to have been discovered that the petitioner company had made secret profits which it had not disclosed and had thus evaded taxa tion. On the 28th August 1953, a report to this effect was made by an Investigation Commission to the Central Govern ment under section 6(4) of Act requesting that the case be investigated and report any case or points in a case referred to it under section S 5. The petitioner contended that (i) the procedure prescribed by the impugned Act in sections 6 and 7 was more drastic than the procedure laid down in sections 37 and 38 of the Indian Income tax Act, and (ii) the provisions of section 34 of the Income tax 'Act were violative of article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the procedure for reference under sub section (4) Of section 5 and the procedure to be followed by the Commission was substantially prejudicial to the assessee than the prescribed procedure under sections 37 & 38 of Act. The procedure thus prescribed in this matter by the Act was substantially similar to those laid down by the Indian Incometax Act.

The respondent, a company registered under the Delhi Shops and Establishments Act, 1954, was carrying on business of manufacturing and selling textiles. It had its main objects in the manufacture of textiles. The main object of the Federation as given in the Memorandum of Association is "to promote Indian business in matters of inland and foreign trade, transport industry and manufactures, finance and all other economic subjects and to encourage Indian banking, shipping and insurance". The main objects of the association are (a) To promote Indian trade in matters relating to inland and Foreign Trade, transport, industry and manufacture, finance, and all allied economic subjects; (b) to secure organised action on all subjects mentioned above. " The object of this Federation is to encourage friendly feeling end unanimity among business community and association on all subject connected with the common good of Indian business. " This was why the question whether the activity of the respondent carried on in these premises is a 'trade, business or profession" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act which, in consequence had no application. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the activities of the appellant Federation carried on by the respondent amounted to "work in connection with, or incidental or ancillary" to trade or business in general within the latter part of the definition of "commercial establishment" given in section 2 (9) of Delhi Shops & Establishments Act 1954; and (ii) that the activities carried on were connected with trade and business, generally. The assessee was a Hindu undivided family headed by one Sri Babu Ausan Singh who was the original founder and owner of what is known as Ausanganj State in the district of Benaras. By a Treaty between the East India Company Nawab Asfuddaula in or about the year 1775, the province of Benaresaras was ceded to British Government. The British Government granted a sanad of Raj to Raja Chet Singh who in turn gave the Jagir of Parganas Seyedpur and Bhittery in perpetuity to Babu Aukan Singh. It appears that in 1796 there were some disputes between Babu Ausausan and the Zamindars in the District and the matter was referred by the Collector of Benarsaras to the Board of Revenue in Calcutta. The quantum of this pension was calculated on the basis of 1/4th of the revenue of the Jagir. By this arrangement, the revenue or land collections of Jagir became payable by the Zamindar direct to the Government and by the grant of the pension, Babu Hat Narain Singh and his successors no longer remained the proprietors of the Parganas or the Jagir and become entitled to merely a pension. The letter by which the amount of pension was determined at Rs. Allahabad to J. The pension was paid regularly from year to year by the Government to Babu Har Narain Singh, and his heirs. During the previous year of assessment 1949 50, the assessee received a sum of Rs. 36,396/ on the footing that it was a regular annual income of the assessee and did not fall within the category of agricultural income tax. The Income tax Officer held that it fell within the definition of agricultural Income tax under section 2(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 as the income was not agricultural income for "although the pension was determination with respect to the quantum of rent collection the rent collections or the land could not be said to be the immediate source of the Pension. The source of this income was a liability undertaken by the government for extinguishing the proprietary rights of the Jagirdar and when the immediate sources of the income were not land or rent collections from land, it is difficult to hold that the receipt of the appellant was agricultural income within the meaning of section 4(3)(viii) of Income tax. He observed that "the language of the letter and this conduct of the parties can only lead to the inference that by this settlement contained in the letter dated July 7, 1837 Babu Harnarain Singh varied from yearto year". The source and character of the receipt are, therefore, altered when a part of the Income tax is appropriated by the appellant as his remuneration, and that is so, notwithstanding that computation of remuneration is made as a percentage of the ' income, a substantial part whereof is derived from lands used for agricultural purposes. The remuneration not being received as rent or revenue of agricultural lands under a title, legal or beneficial in the property from which the income is received, it was not income exempt under section 4 (3)(ix). " The source" of the right in which a fraction of the net income of trust is to be appropriated by him as his remuner is not in the right to receive rent or Revenue of agricultural land but rests in the covenant in the deed to receive remuneration for management of the trust. The income of this trust appropriated as remuneration due is again not the same as the character in which it was received by the assessee as trustee. Both the source and nature of the receipts are, however altered when the part of income of a trust is appropriated for by the Appellant as his salary, and this is so notwithstanding that determination of remuneration was made as percentage of ' the income, the substantial part thereof is derived From lands used in agricultural purposes".
