The Karnataka State Transport Corporation, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and some other private operators filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the vires of section 63(7) of the . The High Court set aside the grant of three out of eleven permits to the Karnataka state Tourism Development Corporation and increased the number of permits granted to the Indian Tourism Development Corpora tion from one to three. The Tribunal took the view that having regard to the rule of preference enunciated by the proviso to section 63 (7), the applications from the 'non preferred ' category had to be excluded as the number Of applications from applicants who were required to be given preference exceeded the number specified in the proviso, and that the grant was set aside. The High court also took the same view. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of some of the private operators that the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court were wrong in distinguishing the decision of this Court in Sher Singh 's case and that in the case of the court interpreted the word 'preference ' occurring in section 47(1 H) in the back ground of the provisions of Chapters IV and IV A of the Act, under the former of which the State transport Undertaking would have preference whereas under the latter the State Road transport Corporation would have a monopoly. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The general scheme of the Motor Vehicles Act in the matter of grant of permits for stage carriages and contract carriages appears to be that except in the cases of a notified route or notified area where under section 68 F(1) the permit has to be necessarily granted to tho State Transport Undertaking, in all other cases, the claims of all eligible applicants must be considered on merits, applying the rules of preference wherever the claims are approximately equal. The proviso to Section 47(I H) for example, provides that in case of inter State route, the Undertaking will have preference in the matters of stage carriage permit. [1015C D] 2. Clause (iv) of section 47 (1 H), for example provides that other conditions being equal, an application for a stage carriage permits from a cooperative society or a person holding a valid licence for driving transport vehicles shall as far as may be, be given priority over applications from individual owners. [ 1015E] 3. The word 'repreference" in section 2(25) is unconstitutional and it is not necessary that the department is able to exercise some control on the functioning of these operators. [10F] 4. Clause(iv) provides for a preference, not to operators of tourist vehicles but to operators or of tourist cars and travel agents. Though the permits to be granted are for tourist vehicles, the preference is confined to operators who of tourist car and travel agent. Although the permits are for Tourist vehicles, it mentions that approval carries with it certain privileges, such as allotment of ex STC vehicles and that it is, therefore, necessary that they should be owning and operating five vehicles as tourist taxies of either indigenous make or acquired from elsewhere regardless of the period in the car hire business or that they must be ex Defence Service personnel, who satisfy certain prescribed conditions. The matter appears to have been left to the total discretion of the Central Government, virtually as we said, pre empting the decision. [1005C E] Sher Singh vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Inspector General of Prisons, Saurashtra. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the order of dismissal was illegal and void on the ground that it contravened article 311(2) of the Constitution. The trial court held that the failure on the part of the competent authority to provide the appellant with a copy of the report of the Enquiry Officer amounted to denial of reasonable opportunity contemplated by article 311 (2). On appeal, the District Judge confirmed the order and dismissed the suit. In second appeal, he contended that the High Court erred in holding that there had been a breach of article 311 as according to him there was no duty to supply a copy thereof. Held, that the appellant was entitled under the Workmen 's Compensation Act, 1906 to compensation from the shipowners not only in respect of his wages but also of the retainer, which must be taken into account as earnings under a concurrent contract of service. The liability to pay salary when it has been fixed arises out of a contract to pay wages. In the present case, the liability to payment of arrears of pay was not a liability arising out of any contract but was a liability in respect Of an actionable wrong other than breach of contract. The decree of the High court decreeing payment of wages was truly a liability and it could not be said that the Government servant was not prejudiced by the non supply of the copy of report of Enquiry Officer. State of Bihar vs Abdul Majid, ; , referred to. Held further, that in the present ease, the appellant had failed to prove that he had been given reasonable opportunity within the meaning of article 313(2). The High Court was right in holding, that there was a breach on his part and that the refusal by the competent officer to provide him with a copies of the reports of the enquiry held against him amounted to violation of article 14.

The appellant 's predecessor in interest, i.e., exhibit 3(b) granted a lease of 96 bighas out of his 400 bighas to one B and the same day he took a fresh lease of the same holding to Samanta and incorporated a map in that lease, i,.e., Exhibit 3(c). The plan, exhibit 3 (b), annexed to this lease deed shows the boundary line between the two leaseholds. As the plan was a part of the lease deed it is clear from the plan that the northern boundary of the leasehold land is the said line. On June 10, 1901, Jugal Kishore Lal gave a fresh grant of lease of 99 bighas out to one Walji Kheta in respect of the said 96 bighas. On the very same day D and M were in possession of the coal mines on the southern side and removed coal from the encroached portion and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portions unworkable. The respondents denied that they had encroached upon any portion of their coal mines. The appellant ' replied that the suit was barred by limitation. The Subordinate Judge held that article 48 of the Limitation Act applied to the suit and that the appellant had failed to prove that the respondents had knowledge of the sinking of the quarries and pits in the encroached land. He further held that the burden of proof was on the respondents to prove the necessary facts. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the findings of fact arrived at by the courts below. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1) the map translated into words indicates that the correct boundary should be a line drawn from the true meeting point of the four villages Pandebera, Jharia Khas, Lodhna and Kujama at a bearing of 82.15; (2) the northern boundaries of the respondents ' leasehold hold was conterminous with the northern demarcation of the appellant ' 's lease hold; (3) the lease of M 's predecessors in interest clearly demarcates the boundary lines between the holdings of the appellants and the respondents, and according to that plan the disputed extent falls within the boundary of their leasehold land in favour of Samanta. Held:(i) The finding of the courts are vitiated by an error of law by the burden on the appellant. (ii) The onus was upon the plaintiff in these suits to prove his knowledge of his father 's possession of a property within three years of the suit, and that is all. If he proves this then to succeed in the plea of limitation the defendant has to prove satisfactorily that the fact that the property was in his possession became known to the plaintiff more than three years prior to the filing of the suits. (iii) The burden of proving that the knowledge of M had been within three months of the date of the filing is on the plaintiff who asserts a right, and it may be, having regard to the circumstances of each case, that the said property was still left in the possession of M.

The appellant was a saw mill carrying on business in Kozihkode in 824 the State of Kerala. One Sankaran was in the employ of the appellant as a crosscutter. It is said that on June 21, 1958 Sankaran came drunk to them mill and abused the Engineer, the Secretary and others and threatened them with physical violence. He was caught hold of by other workmen and taken outside. The appellant served a charge sheet on Sankaran on June 24, 1958 acting out the above facts and asked him to show cause why his services should not be terminated on account of his grave indiscipline and misconduct. Sankaran gave an explanation denying the allegations of fact made against him though he admitted that he had come to the mill at the relevant time for taking his wages for that week. On July 8, 1958, Sankaran was informed that in view of his denial, a departmental inquiry would be held and he was also placed under suspension pending enquiry. The same day Sankaran protested against his suspension and requested that in any case the departmental inquiry should be expedited. As no inquiry was held till July 2, 1958 the appellant terminated the services of Sankaran under r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders without holding any departmental inquiry and the order was communicated to Sankaran. Sankaran thereupon wrote to the appellant to hold the enquiry as early as possible. On June 25, 1958 he terminated the service of Sankaran on the ground that in spite of his refusal, a domestic inquiry would not be held. The Industrial Tribunal held that something seemed to have happened on the afternoon of June 21 and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide exercise of the power conferred. The tribunal also pointed out that no attempt was made before it to defend the action taken under r 18(A) by proving the alleged misconduct. Two witnesses were produced before the Tribunal in connection with the alleged offence but the Tribunal did not rely on them. The Tribunal therefore held that on the facts it could not come to its conclusion that Sankaran had come drunk to the Mill and abused or attempted to assault either the Engineer or the Secretary or other officers. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) It is now well settled that in industrial adjudication relating to termination of service of an employee and has not been accepted by industrial tribunals over a long course of years now and the view taken by industrial Tribunals has been upheld by this Court in the two cases referred to above. The employer could defend the actions under r, 18(b) by leading evidence before the tribunal to show that there was misconduct and therefore the action was taken under rule 18(c). But the Tribunal has pointed out, that the employer did not attempt to do so before it. It satisfied itself by producing two witnesses but withholding the important witnesses on this question. In the circumstances if the tribunal did not accept the evidence of the two witnesses who were produced it cannot be said to have gone wrong. [827 D] (ii) The employer was empowered to take action under r . 18(1) by lead evidence before tho Tribunal to show, that there Was in fact misconduct and hence the action action taken thereunder was bona fide and was not colourable exercise of power under that rule. But the tribunal has pointed Out that the employers did not attempts to do anything before it and it satisfied itself that it had made no attempt to justify before it, It satisfied himself by producing satisfactory evidence; but it seems to have rested upon its right that no such justification was required and therefore having failed to justify its action must suffer the consequences. [829 E F] (iii) The Industrial Court has the right to inquire into the causes that might have led to terminationof service even under a rule like 18(i). But in this case, the tribunal held that the exercise of powers was colourable and it cannot therefore be said that view is incorrect.

The appellants were the lessees of a cinema theatre. The receivers granted a lease of the theatre on certain terms and conditions to two persons, Raval and Faraqui. By an agreement dated November 27, 1954, between Raval and G, both of them agreed that Raval and T shall "execute and register" an agreement in writing incorporating the said agreement with the variation as to rental. The lessees granted a licence to the latter on certain conditions and conditions. "Filmistan" instituted suit No. 149 of 1960 against Raval and two other persons claiming a declaration that it was entitled pursuant to the agreement dated December 1, 1960 to exhibit motion pictures in the theatre. By another agreement dated October 27, 1953, between the parties, Raval & Fara Qui were bound and liable to allow Filmistan to exercise its "exhibition rights" in the Theatre; that Raval & T had no right, title or interest in the cinema theatre, that the defendants in the suit be ordered to hand over vacant and peaceful possession of the cinema films and to exercise their right of exhibiting cinematograph films and entertainment performances etc. in the Cinema theatre and that one Shabeer Hussain Khan Tejabwala had no rights, title and interest in it and that the respondents ' servants and agents were not entitled to have any right to exhibit any picture in contravention of the terms and condi tions of the agreement. The trial court decreed the suit but on appeal the High Court held that the question asked in cross examination of the witnesses for Filmistans intended to secure disclosure of the surrounding circumstances and conduct of the parties in order to show in what manner the language of the document was related to the existing facts, could not be excluded. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that an enquiry into the nature of the legal relationship arising out of the agree ment dated December 27,1954 "was barred by the principle of res judicata and estoppel under the provisions of section 92 of the Evidence Act, since the question was already concluded by consent decree in suit No 149 of1960. HELD : (i) The order passed by the High court is set aside and the Trial Court is directed to proceed and dispose of the suit. [437 B] (ii) The form of the issues Nos. 11, 12 and 13 will be rectified by the learned trial Judge. Filmistenan will pay the costs of the appeal in this Court and in the High Courts. [441 D] (iii) A consent decree accord ing to the decisions of this Court, does not operate as res judicata, because a consent decree is merely the record of a contract between the par ties to a suit, to which is superadded the seal of the court. A matter in contest in a suit may operate as a res judicata only if there is an adjudication by the Court : the terms of section II of the Code leave no scope for a contrary view.

The appellant was acquitted by the Additional Sessions Judge, Chittoor of an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code. The High Court reversed the finding of acquittal and convicted him under section 304 Part I IPC. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the accused had no motive to kill his wife and that his version was more probable than the version of the prosecution. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. An injury of the nature received by the deceased could have been caused in the manner suggested by the prosecution that is, when the deceased was lying on her right side. It is obvious that he must have been upset by the persistent refusal of the brother and mother of the deceased to send her with him to his house. [368E] 2. The accused did not have any deep motive to murder the deceased. It was obvious that she must have had been upset By the persistent reluctance of the father and mother, the deceased, to send his wife with him, to his place. There is no good reason to reject the evidence of P. Ws. 1 to 3 or the evidence on record of P Ws. 4 and 5 who came to the scene soon afterwards, the High Court convicted the accused under section302 and sentenced him as aforesaid. [369C D] 3. The discrepancies were in regard to which of them woke up first, where was the lantern and which of the neighbours came first to the spot on hearing their cries. The Inspector of Police P. W. 15, however, stated that he did not state before him that she saw the accused making a gesture as if he was stabbing the deceased and that the deceased cried out 'Amma. [370E] 4. An offence of murder is an offence which is committed by a person who has been convicted for murder or for murder. The Court cannot interfere with the order of acquittal merely because another view is also possible. [371F G] 5. It stems out of the fundamental principle, of our criminal jurisprudence that theaccused is entitled to the benefit of any reasonable doubt. If two reasonably probable and evenly balanced views of the evidence are possible, one must necessarily concede the existence of a reasonable doubt.[368C D; 369E] 6. The injuries must have be caused in tho manner suggested. It cannot be said that an injury of a nature received from the deceased can have been cause in the way suggested by it that is when the accused was lying down on her left side. [367F G]. 7. The location of the injury was 6 cms below the arm pit on the left side and according to the accused the deceased received the injury when she placed herself between P.W. 3 and the deceased in law. It could not be said, that an injuries of the kind received by him could have caused even if she was standing. It would be possible for the prosecution to make P.Ws. 1, 2 and 3 an old woman of 69 years stated in her evidence that she did not remember if she had told the Police that the appellant made a gestures as if she were stabbing the accused. The medical evidence supported the prosecution version and not the defence version. Merely because the Medical Officer stated that the victim could have received the injuries if she Was standing, it did not follow that the injury could have be received in the circumstances mentioned by the accused.[368E G] 8. The position of law would fail to protect the community if it admitted fanciful possibilities to deflect the course of justice. If the evidence is so strong against a man as to leave only a remote possibility in his favour, which can be dismissed with the sentence 'of course it is possible but not in the least probable ' case is proved beyond reasonable doubt, but nothing short of that will suffice.

The appellant was a Judge of the Supreme Court. He was convicted under section 5(1)(c) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 by the Chief Justice of India and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 1000/ . The High Court dismissed his appeal against that order. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) Section 6(1) (c) is not applicable to the case of a Judge or Chief Justice, of a High Court; (ii) Section 5(2) is attracted and (iii) Section 7(3) is inapplicable. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The President, therefore, being the authority competent to appoint and remove a Judge, of course in accordance with the procedure envisaged in Article 124, clauses 4 and 5 of the Constitution, may be deemed to be the authority to grant sanction for prosecution of a judge under the provisions of Section 6 of the Act in the case where the High Court or the Supreme court is not a vertical superior of any of them, there being no such vertical hierarchy and the Chief Election Commissioner of India having no legal sanction behind it making it justiciable. [299C D] 2. The power to punish a High Judge if one may so describe it, is to be found only in Article 2 18 read with article 124(4) and (5) of Constitution, under which a Judge can be removed from his office by an order of the President passed after an address by each House of Parliament supported by a majority of the total membership of that House and by a minority of not less then two thirds of the members of that house present and voting, has been presented to the President in the same session for such removal on the ground of proved misbehaviour or incapacity. The third most crucial question that falls for decision is whether a Judge is public servant within the meaning of Section 2 of the prevention of Corruption (Act 45 of 1860). [299D] 3.1 In the case, the appellant was the competent authority to remove him from his post. He could be prosecuted with the previous sanction under section 6(i)(c). The question of grant of sanction under Section 6 for the prosecution of superior Judges and the special provisions contained in clauses (4) & (5), of Article 124 read with Article 2, 18, it was suggested, pre sent no difficulty since the President of India could be treated as the competent authori ty to grant permission in accordance. [300E F] 3:2 The power of appointment of Judges of the High Courts and the Supreme Courts under Articles 124(5) and 124(6) read with Articles 2 18, is a clear pointer in the direction that the Parliament has not as yet considered it expedient to enact any such law for the trial and punishment on the charge of corruption of a superior Judge, except by his removal from office in the manner provided in Article124, clauses ( 4) and 5. [302G H] 3(a) The ambit of the enactment is to determine on the basis of the public office held by the public serv ant, which office is alleged to have been abused during the tenure for committing the offence of criminal misconduct under the Act and it is not the fact of continuance in that office or ceasing to hold it which decides the ambit of tho enactment. [303G H; 304A] 3.(b) The power conferred on the President by Article 124(3), even for investigation and proof of any misbehaviour alleged against a superior judge instead of the general law was clearly visualised when the alleged misbehaviour is connected with his office. Can it, therefore be said that while investigation into the allegation of corrup tion for the purpose of removal under Article 124 (5).

The appellant was a member of the Scheduled Caste. Abhoy Pada Saha and Sudhir Kumar Mondal were members of a Scheduled Caste, and Abhiman Pada was declared elected. The respondent challenged the validity of Abhonoy Paada 's election on various grounds. At the hearing of the petition by the Election Tribunal, he challenged the legality of Abhaoy Putta 's elections on various ground. At his election which ensued, Abhokoy P.ada secured 16,730 votes and Sudhir, 15,523 and the former was consequently declared elected, and the appellant filed a petition challenging the validity Of Abhutra Pada ' 's Election Tribunal on various other grounds. The Election Tribunal rejected this contention and dismissed the petition. The High Court held that the Sahas formed a distinct caste wholly outside the Sunri caste and they had been specifically excluded in item 40 for greater safety o prevent them from claiming to be Sunris by reason of their origin, and that the appellant was not a member Of the Scheduled Castes specified in item 39. On appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant: (i) The expression "excluding Saha" in item40 must be read as referring to a smaller caste group within the bigger caste group of Sunirs and was for that reason not a sub caste strictly so called, of Sunri castes; (ii) The respondent 's case was that the word "included" in the expression "including Sahas" meant excluding a smaller Caste group called Sahas. HELD: (1) When a statute says that a thing is to be excluded from another, both things are of the same kind; if one is a caste. the other must be a caste; it follows that when the item excluded Sahas from Sunris, since Sunri is a class group, Saha must equally be another caste group. Therefore, the correct interpretation of the item is that it indicates men of the Suniti caste but not those within that caste who formed the smaller caste groups of Sahas, and, therefore, the proper interpretation of item 40 was that it indicated men of Sunris or not. [390 D E] (2) The Tribunal thought that the respondent 'was a Sunri by caste and had not been proved to belong to the Scheduled caste specified in Item 40 for he said "these Sahas families, within the Sunari caste". The finding that Sahas were a wholly independent caste was altogether irrelevant to the point in issue.

The appellant was the tenant of a flat on the second floor of a building called "Ganga Vihar", Marine Drive, Bombay. The tenancy was a monthly one and the rent being Rs. 215. It was alleged that the appellant wanted to go to the United Kingdom for treatment of his failing eye sight and he got into touch with the police on 1 12 1948 and in conjunction with the latter, a trap was laid for the appellant. The complainant and the Sub Inspec tor were recovered the bunch of keys and documents that were handed over to him by the appellant, namely, the letter handing vacant possession (Exhibit D). The appellant 's wife were also recovered from the rear seat of the car and also some papers, a typed draft of a partnership agreement was tween the complainant and his brother. The police party who were down below ready for the raid held up the car of the appellant and recovered the sum of Rs. 30,500 from the front seat of tile car and handed over the keys to him. As the appellant 'and his wife were leaving the flat, the man who masqueraded as the complain ant 's brother threw off his disguise and disclosed his identity. The Police party, who were up below ready, recovered the bundle of keys from the back seat of a car and gave him Rs. 29,500 to be paid to the appellant on his return to India. The wife was acquitted by the Presidency Magistrate. On appeal, the High Court held that what was received by the accused was by way of pugree but represented capital for 0 12 share in the business and as the com plainant was also to be a caretaker of the flat he was liable to the landlord for the performance of his obligations under the tenancy and sentenced him. On this view, it dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The word "relinquishment" does not occur in the Transfer of Property Act but it is found in many of the Tenancy Acts in various provinces where there are Sec tions which deal with the relinquishment of their holdings by tenants in favour of the landlord by notice given to him in writing. The section in question, it should be further noted, does not speak of relinquishment or giving up of possession,in general terms. The words are "the relinquishment of his tenancy of any premises". The relinquishment of a tenancy is equivalent to surrender by the lessee or tenant of his rights as such. Whether abandonment of a lease would come within the meaning of relinquishment is a question that does not arise in this appeal because in the face of Exhibit D there is no abandonment in the sense that the tenant disappeared from the scene altogether saying nothing and making no arrange ments about his interest and possession under the lease. As in the case of an assignment, the assignoror contin ues to be liable to tho landlord for performance of the obligations under tenancy and this liability is contrac tual, while the assignee becomes liable by reason of privity of estate. The consent of the owner to an assignment is not necessary, in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary. But in the present case there has been no "relation" within the expen tion of section 19, sub clause (1), the conviction under sub clause(2) cannot be sustained. It is set aside and the fine of Rs 30,000 will be refunded if it has already been paid.

The appellant, a partnership firm, was a partnership and the workmen of the Tata Engineering Company were members of the Hindustan Shipyard Limited. The company functions as a consulting organisation and a service industry, and does not manufacture any product or carry on trade. Its work force consists of engineers and supervisors and different categories of workmen. Out of these employees at Bombay, the draftsmen and the administrative staff number 306. These workmen are members of Tata Engineering Co. Ltd., and they served a Charter of Demands in July 1974 on the appellant and as their demands were not accepted and conciliation proceedings proved fruitless, the State Government made a reference of the dispute under section 10(1) (d), Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra for adjudication. The Reference was numbered I. T. No. 292 of 1975. The claim of the Union was resisted by the appellant who maintained that the existing wage scales were fair and reasonable on a region cum industry basis and that it would not be possible for the appellant to bear the additional financial burden if the demands of the union were accepted. But it rejected the demand of the company for dearness allowance on the basis of slab system, because that would have imposed an unacceptable burden on the Appellant 's financial capacity and there was no reason why the existing scheme of dearness allowance should be disturbed when a substantial increase was being made in the level of the basic wage. The Tribunal also noted that after the salaries of the employees had been fixed in the respective scales, senior employees would have to be given some more increments in the new scales according to their completed years of service. Rs. 150/ and Rs. 100/ were added to the pay of every other workman, who belonged to the Union staff, the financial load would increase to Rs.100/ was given to individual workmen of all categories including Draughtsmen, the increased financial load will total Rs. 50/ and above the existing pay scales. The appellant 's application before the Tribunal was contested by the Union contending that the amendment results in the inclusion of a flat increase of Rs.150/ to each workman in the case of Draughtsman and Rs., 100/ and that there was nothing in the body of the award to form the foundation on which the actual figures in the restructured pay scales could be made to rest. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the contention of the appellant that a flat increased to the Pay of each workman was intended in the original wage and, consequently, it fell into the error of amending the award. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the workmen. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the corrigendum was in effect a fresh award and, therefore, falling beyond the jurisdiction of the Tribunal. On behalf of respondent Union it was submitted that the appellant was bound by the order made on the application. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The terms of reference in the State government 's order required the Tribunal to revise the scales of pay and dearness allowance, and there is no mention of giving any ad hoc increase in the basic pay of individual workman. The financial capacity, as the Tribunal observed, constituted one of "the principles which are required to be followed in the fixation of the wage structure". A clear statement of its intention is found in paragraph 22 of the Award where the Tribunal stated: "I only propose to modify the existing structures of the scales with flat increases in each category." [177A B] 2. The award was a composite document in which the several elements of increased wage scales, larger increments, longer span of 20 years for earning increments, dearness allowance at 10% of the Basic wage, besides several other benefits, have been integrated into a balanced arrangement in keeping with what the Tribunal has found to be the financial capacity of the Appellant.

The appellant, Sasamusa Sugar Works Ltd., and its workmen, the respondents an award had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an agreement with the respondents that effect would be given to the wage structure prescribed by the said Award. This agreement was subsequently published in Bihar Gazette as a part of the award. The appellant paid its employees only As. / 10/ per month and that led to the present claim made by the respondents under section 15 of the Act. The respondents contended before the authority that section 15 Of the Act was inapplicable because the rates of wages fixed by the award did not fall within the definition of wages prescribed by section 2(vi) and it also argued, that the claim of the respondents was barred by limitation. Held: (i) The basic assumption made by Mr. Setalvad in contending that section 2 (vi) cannot take in the wages prescribed under the award is not well founded. When an award is made and it prescribes a new wage structure, in law the old contractual wage structure becomes inoperative and its place is taken by the wage structures prescribed by it. In a sense, the latter wage structure must be deemed to be a contract between the parties, because that, in substance, is the effect of industrial adjudication. The true legal position is that when industrial disputes are decided by industrial adjudication and awards are made, the said awards supplant contractual terms in respect of matters covered by them and are substituted for them. That being so, it is difficult to accede to the argument that the wages fixed under the Award cannot be treated as wages under section 2.(vi) of the , before it was amended. The amendment has merely clarified what, in our opinion, was included in the unamended definition itself. In this connection,we may incidentally refer to the decision of this Court in South Indian Bank Ltd. vs A. R. Chacko, ; and V. B Godse, Manager Prabha Mills Ltd., vs R. M. Naick Inspector, under the Payment of Wages Act, (3), the Bombay High Court has interpreted section 2 of the Industrial Disputes Act to include wages directed to be paid by industrial adjudica tion. In the instant case, the basic assumption that section 3(vi)(a) cannot apply in the present case because the wages specified by the Award did not amount to wages as defined by section 1(vi). That, in any event, is, the effect or result of industrial adjudications and awards being made, it was difficult to agree with the argument of the appel lant that the wage prescribed by an award could not be included. In dealing with the question of construing the unamended definitions of the term "wages" it is essential to bear in mind the scope and character of the powers conferred on Industrial Tribunals when they deal with industrial disputes under the provisions of the Indus trial Disputes Act. It is now well settled that unlike ordinary civil courts which are bound by the terms of contract between parties when they dealt with industrial dispute under the , the old statutory wage structure became inoperative and their place is take by the wages structure prescribed under it. Therefore, the essential assumption made in the instant ease was that section 1 (vi)(b) cannot be taken in the wage fixed by an Award. In view of the fact that on references made under section 10(1) of tho Industrial Disputes , terms of employment have constantly been examined by industrial adjudicate and wherever it appeared appropriate to make changes in them, they have been made in accordance with the well recognised principles of fair play and justice to both the parties. Therefore the basic premise made by this Court that section 's 2(vii) cannot come into operation after it was amend ed.

The appellant was a Sub Divisional Officer in the Public Works Department, Pepsu. He was charged under section 409 with having dishonestly removed certain medicines from a hospital which was under his charge and to his own residence. The trial Magistrate held that there was a khalasi Parma by name in the service of the accused at Kehrauli, and that though the thumb impression found in the acquittance roll was that of the appellant himself, he had included a fictitious name in it in the acquittal bill. On appeal by the State to the High Court, Held, that sanction under section 197(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is necessary for prosecuting the appellant under section409 and no sanction is required for a prosecution under that section. Hori Ram Singh vs Emperor (I.L.R. , approved. Shreekantiah Ramayya Munipalli vs The State of Bombay ([1948] L.R 75 I.A. 180), distinguished. ShreeksantiahRamayya Munimalli vs Emperor ([1947] L .R. 75 I A. 180) and Albert Meads vs The King ([1948]. L. R. 75 1. A. 178), referred to. In the present case, there was no order of the Government sanctioning the prosecution, and the question for decision was whether sanction under that s is necessary in all cases in which the official character of the person doing it, those which had held it necessary when the offence was committed while the accused was actually engaged in the performance of his official duties. The sanction was required under section 196(1), Cr. P.C., before the appellant could be prosecuted under section 408 and the absence of such sanc tion is fatal to the maintainability of the prosecution. Shreeka Ramayya vs Emperor, ([1948) L.L R 75 I .A.

The assessee was a public limited company incorporated in the State of Cochin with branches in that State as well as in what was British India and in Travancore State. The main argument was confined to the question whether business losses incurred outside Travancore State could be set off against income under another head, the taxability of income arising from each head being separate. Held, that the words " profits or gains" used in section 10 of the Indian Income tax Act of 1918 were " a loss of profits or gain ". The mere fact that the word " income " is not used does not justify the construction that the intention of the Legislature was to restrict the set off of profits and losses arising under the head business in the two territories, i. e., British India & the Indian States. There it was held that section 10 Of the Indian Act had to be read with section 14(2)(e) and if profits could not be added for the purposes of total income " losses sustained also could not he deducted. Arunachalam Chettiar vs Commissioner of Income tax, Madras, ; , followed. The mere use of the words loss of profit or gains to be set aside against profits and gains would not be sufficient to restrict that scope of the proviso to the profits and loss losses arising in Indian States only to business or to modify the mode of computation under section 10. Arunachalanam Chettiar Chettiar vs C. A. No. 259/58, relied on. The word " profit " is used in the first part of the definition of total world income " and chargeability of total profits under section 3 or the provisions of section 4 where in the case of a resident total income includes income, profits and gain accruing within or without British India or in any Indian State or British India, these losses could not by virtue of the Explanation be deducted from profits made in British India. Arunachalukam Chettiar 's Case, , distinguished.

The first respondent, Shaw Wallace & Co., was incorporated in January 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co. which had been doing business in India for about 60 years. In July 1947 the Private Limited company was converted into a Public Limited Company. The Head Office of the Company was at Calcutta. It had Branches in Bombay, Delhi and Via Madras. The general practice of the company both at the Head office and the Branch Offices appeared to have been to retire its employees at the age of 55 but in some cases the Company in its discretion permitted an employee to continue beyond that age. In September 1959 an agreement was entered into between the Company and its employees for the retirement age of 58 subject to the employees passing a medical examination on reaching the age Of 55 subject to certain employees passing medical examination. The first respondent claimed that no workman should be retired from service before he bad completed 60 years of age. This dispute was ultimately referred to the Industrial Tribunal, Maharashtra. Before the Tribunal the Company resisted the workmen 's claim but submitted that it was agreeable to introduce for its Bombay employees provisions similar to those which had earlier been introduced by agreement for the Calcutta employees retirement at the time of their retirement at 55 subject only to the employee passing a Medical examination on attaining the ageof 55. The Tribunal directed that the age should be 58 but the Company may in its wisdom and with the express or implied consent of the employee concerned continue an employee after he attains that age, and it was also directed that in case any particular region employees have been successful in their claim for fixing the age at 60 this very success is bound to raise in others in the region similar expectations. The Company appealed to this Court by special leave. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the trend in Bombay region had been to fix the retirement date of retirement at 60 years and that it would be impossible to say that the decision of this Court in Dunzlop Rubber Co. Ltd., vs Workmen, ; , relied on by the Tribunal was erroneous on the whole unsound. Held: (i) The age of retirement for workmen in all industries should be fixed at 60. The very few departures from this practice which the Tribunal has mentioned are, in our opinion, wholly insufficient to indicate any slowing down of this trend. What the Tribunal had failed to notice is that instances which may justify a revision of the judicial opinion expressed on an earlier occasion about a particular trend must be strong and unambiguous and they must speak for the period both before and more particularly after the previous finding had been recorded in the matter. (ii) The Tribunal has referred to these observations but has brushed them aside in a way for which we find no justification. (iii) The approach adopted by the Tribu nal was not very commendable, and that its present conclusion that what was said by itself on an Earlier occasion and was confirmed by this Court was in fact inaccurate. If this Court had erred in making those pronouncements it would he first to admit such mistakes and to correct the error. (iv) The contention of the workmen that the Tribunal 's finding that in all the awards in recent times in various concerns in Bombay Region the trend had been about fix the retire age at 55 or 58 is not challenged before this Court, was rightly rejected by the tribunal.

The first respondent, a company incorporated in the year 1961 and to report to the Company Law Board inter alia "all the irregularities and contravention in respect of the provisions of or of any other law for the time being in force and the person or persons responsible for such irregularities and contravened. " The first respondent passed an order on May 19, 1965 under section 237(b) of the appointing authority appointed 4 persons as Inspectors for investigating the affairs of the Barium Chemicals Ltd., appellant No. I before us since its incorporation in the years 1961 and 1962 to report the Company law Board interalia "all irregularities and breach in respect thereof". The first appellant challenged the order on the ground that it was made by the Chairman of the Board and not by the Board; and that the provisions Of section 237 (b) were void as offending articles 14 and 19(1)(g) of Constitution. Held, that the power conferred on the Central Government by section 237 of the Act to order an investigation and delegated by it to the company Law Board is administrative and that if the grounds are disclosed by the board the Court can examine them for considering whether they are relevant. The powers are exercised for ascertaining facts and, therefore before they are finally known, all that is necessary for the exercise of the powers is the opinion of the board that there are circumstances which suggest to it that fraud and other kinds of mismanagement mentioned in sub cls. (i) to (iii) of section 10E read with section 642(1) clear and that distribution of the work of the company being merely a matter of procedure the order of the Chairman allocating the power under section 236(b), to himself did not amount to sub delegation of the power of the Company Board. The power is exercised for considering facts and therefore before them are finally deemed known, they all that was necessary for exercise of this powers is opinion of Board that there were circumstances suggesting that fraud or other kinds mentioned in subs. (4A) added subsequently to section 10 E enabling the solidarity of the Boards to be broken. The Central Government has power to constitute the Company Court, to delegate its functions to the Board but it had no power to authorise the Chairman to sub delegate this function to himself and consequently the company law Board (Procedure) Rules, 1964 made by that Government on February 1, 1964 delegating the function of the Committee under section 239 to the Chairman are ultra vires the and the impugned order is invalid.

The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to three years ' rigorous imprisonment. The High Court, on appeal, held that the presumption that they were dacoits ought not to have been drawn since the circumstances did not admit the drawing of such a presumption in the case, according to law, but it was always to start with the lesser presumption and draw the higher presumption only when there is some other evidence to show the complicity of the persons in the crime itself. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The proper inference was drawn in this case. It must not be forgotton that the offence was committed at night by as many as 20 persons or more. [723 E] The time gap in some cases is as short as two days and in some others it is not more than five days. In two cases only the time gap is about 19 days. Even then, the time is too short for original offenders to have disposed of the property to these appellants Or to have left the goods in their custody till such time as the original offenders could take them away. [777 E H] The law advocated by Mr. Chari is not correct. If there is other evidence, to connect an accused with the crime, it however small, the finding of the stolen property with him is a piece of evidence which connects him further with the offence. There is then no question of presumption. [779 E F] In some cases there may be other elements which may point to the way as to how the presumption may be drawn. They need not be stated here for they differ from case to case.

The petitioners were contending that in substance manufactured by them did not come within Rule 2(x)(2) and there were some correspondence in this regard, when the competent authority held that the substance manufactured was manufacturing only those thinners which contain only liquid substance, like ecotone, ethyl acetate SDS etc. and not all solubles. The petitioners contended that in essence manufactured by themselves did not fall within Rule 1(x) (2), and there was some correspondence between them when the Government decided to include the substance as poison and regulated the decision in one State to include substance as medicine, and regulated and the decision of another State to exclude the substance from the list of poisons. The respondents contended that the petitioners were a manufacturer of 'thinner ' within Rule l(x), and that there were correspondence in the regard, and when the authority held the substance was manufacturing it would come within the definition of "thinter" as contained in Rule 2 (x)(ii) of the Rules. The authorities rejected the contentions of the petitioners and quashed the notification. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of both Sections 2 and 5 of the , are not hit by any consti tutional limitation. [225G] 1.2 The provisions contained in neither Section 2 nor Section 5 nor the impugned notification are hit by Article 14 or Article 19(1)(g) of Constitution. The writ petition accordingly fails and it is dismissed. Rule nisi is discharged. No order as to costs.

The appellants were partners of a firm styled "Bhojaji Sobhachand" carrying on business at Madras as importers of yam and also as agents and adathias. Sobhachand, one of the partners of Bhojaji Sobha Chand with 16% share in the profit and loss was the father of Seshmal, Ramniklal and Lakshmichand, partners of the appellants. In the books of account of the appellant which were main tained according to the mercantile system there was a current sarafi account in respect of their transactions with the Bombay firm in which were credited the funds transmitted from Bombay in respect thereof. The Income tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that the debt did not arise in the course of the assessee 's business as chemists and druggists nor in the Course of their money lending business. He held that the debts did not fall within section 10(2)(xi) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, and that the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the amount of Rs. 2,68,385 written off by the assessee in their books of accounts as irrecoverable was not one incurred in the way of money lending or for any other purpose as preferred to para 7 above. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed this order but in appeal the Tribunal held that on the facts and circumstances of the case the Tribunal erred in disallowing a sum of Rs 2, 68,385/ written off as irrecoverable. On further appeal by the Department to the High Court it was contended that there were three important circumstances which appear from the order of the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner and the Income tax officer from which it may be inferred that the advances made by the appellants to the Bombay firms were not in respect Of loans in the ordinary course of money lent business of the asses see. The Tribunal rejected this contention and held that there was no question of "locating any portion thereof as between the business of money lenders or for anything other purpose" as preferred ' to para. 7 above, and therefore the amount was allowable under section 10 (2) (xi). On appeal by special leave: Held, that before the question may be answered it is necessary to call for a supplementary statement of the Case from the Tribunal. The statement submitted by the Tribunal is also inadequate. It contains only a summary of the business relations between the appellants and the Bombay Firm, a statement as to the amounts due at the end of each year at the foot of the account, the interest if any charged and a summary or summary of orders made by Income tax Officers, the Appellate Assist ant Commissioner and the Tribunal, and the High Courts. The statements submitted by tile Tribunal are also inadequate and it contains only summary of business relations. It is true as contended by the learned Counsel for the Revenue that the conclusions reached by the tribunal are not supported by proper discussion of the material before it. It cannot be denied that the findings reached by tho Tribunal are findings of fact and those findings are supported by the evidence on record. The tribunal has found that the monies sent by the appellant to the Madras firm were not loans made in the normal course of its money lending trade, nor in respect o any other business of assessee. As this is the finding with regard to the whole of the amount it cannot be deny that the finding reached by tile tribunal are findings Of fact and these findings are based on evidence on the record.

The petitioners were the owners of certain lands which were acquired by the respondents under the provisions of Sections 17 and 19 of the Bangalore Development Act, 1976. Under the provisions Of Section 36 of the Act, the period during which any action or proceeding to be taken in pursuance of the said declaration is stayed by an order of a Court shall be excluded. The petitioners filed writ petitions challenging the acquisition on the ground that the awards were not made within two years of the notification making the declaration under Section 4 of the Land Acquisition Act. The High Court dismissed the petitions holding that the award was not made in time and directed status quo with regard to possession of the lands in question. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that as the awards in these cases had not been made within the stipulated time, the entire acquisition proceedings had lapsed. That contention was repelled along with certain other contentions in the judgment of the High Court which is sought to be impugned before this Court. Dismissing the Special Leave Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The relief under Article 136 of the Constitution is discretionary and a petitioner who approaches this Court for such relief must come with frank and full disclosure of facts. If he fails to do so and suppresses material facts, his application is liable to be dismissed. [566D] 2. In the instant case, the Special leave petitions are liable to have been rejected. It is well settled in law that the relief under article 136 of Constitution is discretion and a petition who approaches the Court for relief must fail with frank & full disclosure thereof of facts.[566F] 3. The interim orders have a direct bearing on the question raised and the non disclosure of the same certainly amounts to suppression of material facts. On this ground alone, the special leave petitions were liable to he rejected.

The respondents made applications under section 33 C(2) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 praying for determination and computation of their benefit to which they were entitled under the Desai award as modified by the Labour Appellate Tribunal Decision (Bank Disputes) Award of June 1962. The Desai award dealt with the method of adjustment in the scales of pay fixed by it from para 5.329 onwards. It divided the employees of banks with which it was concerned in two groups. The first group consisted of workmen who were drawing basic pay on January 1, 1962 according to scales of wages provided by the ALL India Industrial Tribunal (Bank Dispute) Award 1953 as modified and were not thus drawing basic salary on the footing of scales of Pay provided by that award. In the first case the Desai Award provided that these employees would first be fitted in the appropriate scales provided in the Sastry award as amended from time to time and thereafter they would be fitted In the new scale applicable to them under the Sastry Award as modified. The second group consisted Of workmen who on January1, 1962 were employed in banks which were not governed by the provisions of the Sastry Act as modified, except (i) those who were not covered by the Sastry Awards as modified on January Ist, 1962 and (ii) those whose basic pay as on January 31, 1950. The respondents made application under section33 C(1)(d) of that Act praying for fixation and computation Of the benefit to be which they had been entitled under Desai Award as they were not satisfied with the fixation of their pay by the appellant bank under para 5, but the Desai Tribunal held that the adjustment basic pay in the new scales was not to exceed what point to adjustment would give an employee on January I 1962. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the respondents that the adjusted basic pay was to be as on 1st January 1959 and that the adjustments were made in accordance with clauses (a), (b) and (c) of cl. (iv) and the adjustment of basic pay under para. 5.356 of the Desai ' award was not therefore bad. HELD : The adjusted basic Pay in cl. 5 has to be taken as on 31st January, 1959. This follows from the fact that the workman 's basic pay is more than what point of adjustment would given under cl. 6 which provides for actual calculations starts with the words "subject to rules (i), (ii), (iii) and therefore the actual calculations made under el. 5 must be subject to clauses (i). [903 H; 902 A B] The adjusted Basic Pay in clause (ii)(b) has to he taken as the on January l, 1959, sub cl. 4(a) read with sub cl.(c) and have to be added, but this is again subject to the provisions Of cls. (i); (ii). The adjustment of the basic pay has to take place as on December 1, 1960. This is again so subject to cl. 903(b), (iv). [ 902 E F] Prakash Chand Mehra vs Union of India, ; , followed.

The appellants, who were the owners of a hotel in Calcutta, challenged the grant of four acres of land out of Begumbari Compound to India Hotel Co. The High Court held that the decision to lease the Begumbar land to the Taj Group of Hotels was taken on February 12, 1981 and that it was not forgotten that if the land was to be allotted to the Zoo logical Garden upon the terms set out in the two letters, there would still remain sufficient land for accommodating the existing facilities. The appellants filed an appeal before this Court against the decision of the High Court. On behalf of the appellants it was contended that the second Cabinet Memorandum dated September 9, 1981 on which date the Government took the final decision to grant the lease made no mention of the needs and interests of the Zooo or the facilities provided in the Begambari land for the Zoological Garden and there was no way by which the Government could divest the ZOogical Garden of the land except by a procedure known to law such as acquisition or requisition. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The proposed hotel is a Garden Hotel and there is perhaps every chance of the ecology and environment improving as a result of planting numerous trees all around the proposed hotel and the removal of the burial ground and burial ground for rubbish. [260F] 1.2 In the face of all these material facts, it cannot be seriously contended that there was an infinite variety of coniderations which may have to be taken into account by the Government in formulating its policies and it is on a total evaluation of various considerations which have weighed with the Govern ment in taking a particular action, that the Court would have to decide whether the action of the Government is reasonable and in public interest. [262G H] 1:3 The provisions of the Bengal Public Parks Act have no relevance to the question of the power of the government to transfer the Begumberland land to a Taj Group o f Hotels. The Chief Minister 's attention was expressly drawn to the Managing Committee 's first Resolution expressing its opposition to the proposal to give the land for construction of a Five Star Hotel on the Begangumbari land as a final decision, to the hotel group to start a Five star hotel, which according to the Government was a prime need to the city of Calcutta. The next question is whether the Government of West Bengal acted with probity in not inviting tenders or in not holding a public auction but negotiating straightaway at arm 's length with the Taj group of Hotels. [263A B] 1 :4 The provisions Of the BengalPublic Parks Act, 1904 have no relevancy to the ques tion of the powers of the Govern ing to transfer Begumbri land to an Taj Group. The Government was quite alive to the need for expan sion of the zoo when they decided to grant four acres Of Begumbli land which was not used for the main purpose of theZo for the construction of Five Star Hotels. The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, carried on the business of banking and hence the gifts were valid. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee that he did not make valid gifts aggregating Rs. 1,50,000 in favour of his sons and grand sons by his letter dated 1.1.1957. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that there was no valid gift on the date of the entries, then it could not be held that subsequently, when the money was transferred by further entries in the same books, it resulted in a valid gift. In reference, the High Court held that the sum of Rs. 67,560/12 was rightly included in the assessee 's net wealth and held that under section 123 of the , in case of gifts of movable property, the transfer may be effected by delivery. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Tribunal right ly held that a sum of money was properly included in his net wealth; (2) the gift was not valid; and (3) the mere book entries were not sufficient in that case to constitute valid gift, and as there was nothing to show that the interests which were credited in the accounts of the minor donees by the firm which carried on money lending business also were fictitious. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in answering the question in the manner it did. [129E] 2.1 In case there was not sufficient cash balance from out of which the amount gifted could be physically given to the donee more entries in his books of account in the form would not constitute delivery of possession over the gifted property to the donor and gift in such case will not be valid. [130F] 2:2 The High court was in wrong in answering that question in view of the fact that the assessee had made a valid gifts of the value of Rs,50000. Where the assessee has a credit amount with firm or with family or with a banking company and that sum is available to that firm or the company or H.U.F. on the dates of the gift, then a valid transfer by book entries might be possible but where a sum was not available with the firm or family or a company which was not a banking Company or which had no overdraft facility, by mere book entry even though there was acceptance of that gift by the donee would not effectuate a valid Gift. [131G] 2 :3 The High Courts were in error when answering the ques tion in the negative. [132F] 3:1 In the instant case, except to the extent indi cated above, the entries in books could not effectuate gifts. As there was none of these facts it could be said that the donee had retained the possession and enjoyment of the property to his entire exclusion of the donor or, to the entire exclusion, of the gifted donor in any benefit to him by contract or otherwise.

The Orissa Superior Judicial Service (senior branch) is a combined cadre consisting of officers holding purely judicial posts as well as posts which are essentially administrative in character. It consists of eight district and sessions judges, two additional district and Sessions Judges, secretary to government in law department, superintendent and legal remembrance and ex officio Additional District and Sessions judges. In view of article 229 of the Constitution the power to appoint the secretaries to the Government is that of the Governor. Under the Government of India Act 1935, the power of transfer a district judge from one post to another was that of Governor though that power was always exercised in consultation with the High Court and by large on the recommendation of the High court. Obviously when the Governor promulgated the Orissa Superior judicial Service Rules 1963 he proceeded on the basis that the power could be transferred from one cadre to another whether as a Judge or to one of the posts in the secretariat was in his hands. The High Court was anxious that a judicial officer occupying one of these administrative posts enumerated above should not, in the interest of judicial work continue in that post for an unduly long time. The State Government implemented the orders in question on March 6 1967 and on October 10 1966, the Chief Secretary to the government of Orissa, the Home Secretary to Government of Orissa transferred all the officers mentioned above for being posted as district and Session judges or addl. district Judges as the case may be, the government turned down those requests on one ground or the other. The order of the State Government was set aside by the HighCourt in appeal. In these appeals by special leave it was contended that (1) the order of transfer passed by the State of Orissa is unsustainable because (a) the power under article 235 of the constitution is exclusively that of a Governor; (b) the Chief Justice is only concerned with the appointment, promotion and posting to the cadre which power is vested in the High Courts under article 233, though in consultation it with the high Court and (c) the control given to the High courts over district courts under that Article includes control over officers who preside over those courts. HELD: (1)(a) The High court must be held to have had no authority to act as law secretary, superintendent or legal remonstrancer and member sales tax tribunal respectively on and after October 10, 1966 is set aside. [158 D] (b). The order transferring the District Judges already appointed or promoted and posted in the cadre must necessarily be outside the power vested in it by article 235 as the control vested in that Article include control over the officers who presided over those Courts. [159 E F] (c).

The appellant, a co sharer in the two brothers and brother 's sons of the vendors, had been in occupation of agricultural land. The respondent State issued a notification under section 15(1)(a) of the Punjab Pre emption Act, 1913, which was later amended by the Punjab Amendment Act, 1960. The appellant challenged the constitutional validity of section 15 on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution. It was contended that the suit land belonged to more than one co sharers and had not been sold jointly by all the co shar ers jointly. The High Court upheld the constitutional vires of section15(1) (a) and held that there was no infringement of Article 19(1). In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the suit lands belonged to a more than two co sharener and had been sold separately by all co shar erers jointly, he was entitled to claim the right of pre emption under clause 'fourthly ' of section 14(1), and that the interpretation placed by the High Court on the expression 'other co shares ' in section 15 (1)(b) requires reconsideration as it leads to certain anomalous situation e.g., a sister who is a co tenant can claim pre empt while her brother cannot or a daughter 's daughter of the vendor can claim preemption but not the son. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The expression ' other co sharors ' in clause 'Fourthly ' in cl. 'Fourthally ' of Section 15(i)(b), refers to only those co shar es who do not fail under clause "First" or 'Secondly ' or 'Thirdly 'of section 15.(1) of tho Act. The use of the expression "other co seniorityers" in clause fourthly conveys the possibility of their being co shared also. The right of preemption to co sharpers is held to be intra vires the Consti tution. [123B] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant sought to exercise the right under section15 (1) by virtue of his pre em tion conferred on him by that provision. He was not a co accused in the suit. The fact that he had been a co Accused in the earlier suit would not make any difference because the earlier suits were pending in this Court and the High Courts had held against him. [124C D] 3.2 In the present case, it is difficult to hold that this Court intended to deny the right to pre em pption of those kinsfolk even if they happened to be co shar lers. The object of the Legislature was to deny to the right which was conferred on a specified family members of the seller or vendors who were specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section fifteen(1 )(b). [124E] 3:3 In the context, it becomes clear that the legislature desired to confer the right on specified family member of the ly or vendors in the first three clause of section '15(i) (b) even if there were two co owners jointly and had no interest in the land or property sold or a part thereof. The relations in the second three clauses are held to have been denied the right by the appellant. [125F] 4.1 The expression " other co divided" was used in the fourth clause of the said provision to ensure that no co sharper is left out. Once conferment of the right in favour of co shars was considered to be a reasonable restriction on the right, acquire and dispose of property under Article 19 (1).

The respondent No. 2, a Hindu widow, had two wives. The first wife was the adopted son of the second respondent by name Anand Babu. In February 1985, during the pendency of the special leave petition, the adoptive mother died. The respondents filed a suit for title and injunction. While each of the parties had taken such stand in the litigation a compromise was brought about on 21.8.1987 between the father and his two sons and the same was filed in this Court. The terms of the compromise stipulated payment of Rs. 1 lakh by the father to each of his two son in lieu of relinquishment of their interest. When the matter was listed before the Court for recording of the compromised, Sudarshan Gupta, second respondent maintained that he had not been paid Rs.1 lakh as stipulated and he had no intention to accept the compromise. The alienees have now been brought on record unders order of this Court, which is in accord with the principle indicated in the said decision and are of the view that as the compromise petition is genuine and lawful the same has to be acted upon. Allowing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The alienations are for about a purported consideration of Rs 4 lakhs. The sale deeds indicate that a sum of Rs, 1 lakh had been received earlier and a net amount of Rs 77,124 out of the consideration money under these documents has been paid before the registering authority. The transferees have admittedly been in possession of the property from the date of the sales which is more than three years old by now. Admittedly, the transfers are pendente lite. In fact if the compromise is valid and binding the alienor respondent No 2 had no interest in the property to part with in view of the stipulation in the compromise that on receipt of Rs 1 lakh he relinquished his entire interest in it. The alienation has made an attempt to hold out that there were agreements for sale prior to the compromise for which there is no acceptable evidence. [541D E] 2. The transferee had no right created under the alleged sale deeds. Their possession is without authority of law. Ordinarily, they would have been liable to account for mesne profits. In view of this fact that there was the allegation of payment of money by the alienees. He sought to rely on certain decisions which on being referred to were found to be totally inapplicable to the facts of the case. On the other hand, it is found that a similar question arose before the Orissa High Court in the case of Bhoja Govinda Maikap & Anr. vs Janaki Dei & Ors., AIR (1980) Ori. 108 where the power of the court under Order 23, rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the face of an objection of one of the party to the compromised was considered.

The appellants, workmen and the respondents, felt aggrieved because of the first proviso to section 49 of the , they were not entitled to the sickness benefit for the first two days of sickness except in the case of a spell of sickness following, at an interval of not more than 15 days, the spell of sick leave for which sickness benefit was last paid. The Company also contended that there was no practice of giving any such sick leave in the industries in Baroda or in the State of Gujarat. In the case in which the claim for sickness benefit had been rejected by the Tribunal, it was stated that the workmen of the company get the benefit of sick Leave upto 21 days and that the reasonableness of the demand could not be examined by the Company Tribunal. The Tribunal awarded 7 days sick leave with full pay and dearness allowance to the workmen. In appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appellants it was contended that as the benefits of sections 47 and 49 of tile Act were already admissible to workmen in Baroda with effect from December 14, 1969, and they were quite adequate, the Tribunal committed an error of law in granting the additional benefits mentioned above. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The benefit of sickness leave was lost when the Act was made applicable to the region from December14, 1969. That was obviously under a mistaken impression of the sickness benefits which the Act allowed for, as has been shown, it does not deal with all aspects of the claim of sickness benefit and does not, at any rate, provide for the grant of leave on full emoluments during the period of the workman 's physical incapacity to earn his normal wages because of his sickness. It is difficult to see however, that the benefit that the workers will get under this Act can affect the question of sickness Leave being provided for the workmen.[83C D] 2. The scheme of the benefits admissible under the Act cannot be said to cover the work men 's demand for sick leave to the extent allowed by the tribunal. [86E F] 3. The Act does not in fact deal with the question whether sickness leave can affect tho question of maternity leave being provided to the workers. It has to be appreciated that a workman is prevented from earning the normal daily wages during the periods of his illness and there is no justification for the argument that the rate of benefit at about half his wage, under the , Act should be considered sufficient so as to deny him the bene fit of sick leaves on full pay for a period of 7 days when he is certified by a competent medical officer to be ill for that or a longer period. It would thus appear that the appellants have not been able to show that the awards in question are illegal or unjust; or would adversely affect the economy or the indus trial peace, or lead to imbalance in the conditions of service in other industrial establishments. [83E F; 84A B] 4. The appellants have failed to show as to how the awards were illegal or inequitable. or would prejudicially affect the efficiency and progress of the industry. It appears that it was not necessary for the Tribunal to award the benefit under the provisions of the Act, to award a benefit of the sick leave on the full emoluments for a certain period of seven days when the workman is certified as by a medical practitioner. [84B C] 5. The question regarding adequacy of the Sick Leave has been examined by this Court in Technological Institute of Textiles vs Its Workmen and others, ; , referred to.

The appellant was detained under the , by an order of detention passed on the 8th June, 1955. The grounds of detention were served on him along with the order of his detention. He challenged the validity of the order based on the ground that the detaining authority acted merely at the instance of the police who were in league with the Goan National Movement and to take up professionally the cause of persons in the position of Carlos. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The obligation to furnish particulars and duty to consider whether the disclosure of any facts involved therein is against public interest cannot be so exercised as to nullify the constitutional right of representation and an obligation to communicate cannot be implied in these circumstances. It was not necessary for the detaining authorities to have felt that the grounds furnished were so vague as to hamper him in his right to make a representation under article 22(5) and section 7 of the Act. The necessity for such a communication would arise only if the detenue, feeling the grounds to be vague, asks for particulars. But in the absence of any such request by the detenue the non communication of the decision cannot be held to have hampered his constitutional right Of representation and the obligation to supply particulars and the duty to considered whether the disclosed of any fact involved therein was against public interests. The requirement for such communication would depend on the facts of each case. In the present case there is no merit in this contention. (ii)The order of preventive detention was made without any real application of mind by the detaining Authority, that the authority acted only at the behest of the Police who were not in lete with the DeSte but also at the time of filing the affidavit. The fact that be bad made no such application for particulars is therefore a circumstance which may well be taken into consideration, in deciding whether the grounds can be considered to be invalid. (iii)The requirement for making a representation against his detention cannot be said to have been hampered by the non supply of particulars and failure to furnish the duty and to consider the sufficiency of such particulars would not vitiate the order.

The respondent was a commissioned officer in the Indian Army and was attached to the Army Ordnance Corps Training Centre, Secundrabad. It was alleged that on April 4, 1958 he committed acts of gross misconduct. The allegations were as follows: "Knowing Kumari Prakash as the daughter of a brother Officer Rao assisted her in going away from her parents protection and planning to run away with a sepoy. " He was charged with having committed acts amounting to gross misconduct under section 161 Indian Penal Code, 1860. The trial court held that the conduct of the respondent was most unbecoming of an officer and ordered administrative action to be taken under r. 14 of the Army Rules, 1954. On appeal by the Union of India, the High Court set aside the order of removal from service on the ground that r.14 of the said Army Rules was ultra vires the . The Union of lndia appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The words "subject to the provisions of this Act" occurring in section 19 makes section 19 subject to section 45, and the Central Government has thus no power to remove a person from the service in derogation of the provisions Of section 45. But the power under section 19 is an independent power. Although section 19 uses the words "Subject to the provision of this . Act", it speaks of removal of a personfrom the service. Section 45 provides that on conviction by court martial an officer is liable to be cashiered or to suffer such less punishment as is in this Act mentioned. For removal from the Service under section19 of the read with r. 13 of the Rules, the Central Govern ment may remove a "person from the serv ice". Rule 14 is such a rule : it is, therefore, not ultra vires. [450 B] (ii) The word "subject" occurring therein in section19 makes section lain that there should be rules and subject to the other provisions of the Act and such rules, the central Government may dismiss or remove from the services any person subject to this Act. It follows that there may be a valid rule where under, subject to other provisions Of the Act, the C.P.C., the Central Govt. may remove from service any person "from the serv ices" and r.

The Standing Committee inspected the premises of the company but in their order they have given very scanty facts, They do not say whether the tea is crushed, processed or treated chemically to convert it into a marketable commodity.
