The petitioner was detained under section 3(2) of the , on the ground that he 's activities were prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The grounds of detention stated that there was indiscriminate firing in the main market area of Katras created great panic and alarm in the area. The incidents alleged against him and his associates were also reported by the police. The petitioner/appellant made representation on 22nd January, 1986 and the appellant was informed that the said representation was rejected. Thereafter, the petitioner 's matter was referred to the Advisory Board but he was not given any hearing. By letter dated 22nd February, 1986 the petitioner/ appellant was intimated that the representation was considered rejected. The appellant/petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed without any speaking order. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the petitioner that the order of preventive detention could only be justified against a person in detention if the detaining authority was satisfied that his release from detention was imminent and the order was necessary for putting him back in jail. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The principles applicable in these types of preventive Detention cases have been discussed in the decisions of Suraj Pal Sahu vs State of Maharasthra & Ors., W.P. (Crl.) No. 2 96/86 with W. P. Judged on the basis of 911 the said principles there is no ground for interference with the order. [910G] Rameshwar Shaw vs District Magistrate, Burdwan & Anr., ; and Ramesh Yadav vs District magistrate Etah and others, though there was a statement to the effect that the detenu was in jail and was likely to be enlarged on bail. But on what consideration that opinion was expressed is not indicated especially in view of the fact that the petitioner was in custody of that there Was any real danger of his release. Nor does it appear that before the service there was consideration of this aspect properly. [936C] Rameshwar Yadav vs State, W.p. (Cr.) No 2 96 of86 with Crl A. 353/86 and W.A. 353 of 1986 with W P.J. Judging on the principle applicable in the instant case, the continued detention of the detenu under the Act is not justified. [948D] Rameshwar Sahu vs District Magis trate Burdwan & Ors. ; , referred to.

Section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968 confers an arbitrary and uncanalised power without any criteria for guiding the discretion of the Administrator. The section does not provide nor is any rule brought to our notice which enjoins upon the Administrator to give a hearing to dealer who seeks permission under this Section and give reasons in case he decides to refuse the permission. No rules have been framed prescribing the conditions or circumstances under which the permission can be granted or refused (1) 955SCI/76 854 (2) 956SCI/75 has been framed nor any particular guide line has been expressly indicated in sec. 28 by reference to which the power conferred on the Administrator could be exercised by the Administrator, but that is not decisive of the matter. It cannot be disputed that sec.28 is part and parcel of the entire scheme of Gold Control as envisaged by the Act and the object of the enactment and the scheme affords sufficient guidance to the Administrator in the matter of exercising his discretion under that section. The main object in putting the Act on Statute Book as indicated by its long title is "to provide, in the economic and financial interests of the community, for the control of production, manufacture, supply, distribution, use and possession of, and business in, gold ornaments and articles of gold and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto. " In other words, the several restrictions that have been put on the activities of the traders doing business in gold will have to be viewed from the aforesaid perspective. It is also clear that the restrictions which have been imposed in secs. 28 are meant to prevent circumvention of other provisions of the Act. Therefore, in our view the objective, the policy and the Scheme of the , together with the necessity to ensure prevention of circumvention by the other provisions Of the Act afford more than sufficient guidance. The object is to prevent the circumvention, of other provision of the . The objective, therefore, the Policy and the Schemes of the impugned Act together with necessity to ensuring prevention of circumstances of circum potance of the other provision in the Act affords sufficient guidelines to the administrator in the matters of exercising the power of discretion conferred on him under sec. In fact section 5(1) requires that the Administrator should have regard to the policy, and purposes of the 'Act in making his orders. Moreover against his order under that Section a revision lies to Central Government which implies that he will have had to make judicious use of his power or discretion and any improper exercise is liable to be corrected by a higher authority. If that be so it cannot be said that unfettered or uncanalised or arbitrary power has been conferred upon the Administration under sec . Moreover, regard must be had to be the nature of the restrictions imposed by the section. It does not impose any blanket or 956 absolute prohibition upon a dealer from carrying on money lending, banking or any other business in the same premises in which he carries on business as a dealer but he is prevented only from carrying out business as money lender or banker on the security of any article, ornament or both unless authorised by the administrator. Even the restriction in the case of a third person in carrying on business in a licensed premises of the dealer and while implementing such limited restrictions or granting relief against the same he will be guided by the policyand purposes of that Act and by the prime consideration that circumvention Of the other Provisions of the provisions of section 28 shall not be premitted. Having regard to this position which obtains in the cases sec. 27 cannot be struck down on the ground of excessive delegation of legislative power and its validity has to be upheld. [955H; 956A B] Harakchand Ratanchand Banthias vs Asst. Collector of Central Excise Poona, II Division while declaring unamended sec.27(6) in several of its clauses referred to certain concepts which Administrator was required to take into account, and these concepts were regarded as indefinite, uncertain and vague.

The appellants, who were the trustees of a temple in Eragudi village, Tiruchirappalli district, claimed to be the trustees for an alleged Pachai Kandai Udayavar Temple at Eravudi. The properties covered by the grant bad been granted in Inam to the original grantee burdened with the obligation of performing certain services in a Matam. In appeal to this Court by special leave: HELD : (i) The question whether on facts proved in the present case an inference can be drawn that the previous manager or trustee had been removed from management of the temple de facto, has not been discussed by the High Court. [133 E F] Gnanasambanda vs Rachaikantha Udayavar Devasthanam, Eravanar, Erahgudi, and Damodar Das 's case (2) In the present ease, the question which arose for decision was whether article 134B applied to a case where debuttar property had been sold in an execution sale, and the Privy Council held that it did not. [134 F] (iii) The High Court was right in decreeing the appellants ' suit in its entirety.

The respondents, who had retired from the firm and who continued to be a partner jointly issued a notice to the District Magistrate, Jammu, asking him to vacate the premises of Apsara Theatre. The District Magistrate rejected the said request by a detailed order dated April 21, 1979. It was found that the licence in respect of the Apsa Theatre had been granted to one Ved Gupta and that it shall remain in force until March 31, 1970, provided that Shri Ved Gupta or any person to whom with the consent of the licensing authority, the licence is transferred, continues to own or manage the cinematographs used ill the said Apsar Theatre. On December 3, 1975, the respondents filed a suit against the appellants and seven others by seven of the partners including Krishan Kumar for a declaration that the Cinema licence dated July 22, 1969 issued by the District Judge Jammu (8th defendant) for exhibition of cinematographs in the building known as Apsra Theatre, Gandhi Nagar, Jammu is the property of the firm Apsana Theatre and for a prohibitory injunction restraining them from interfering with the running of the Theatre by the plaintiffs and also for a mandatory injunction restraining the appellants from interfering in any manner with the exhibition by the Plaintiffs of cinematograph films in the premises known as "Apsara Cinema". It has further been submitted that even on receipt of the order of temporary injunction, it had become impossible for him, for the time being, to operate the cinema licence with effect from the date of the said letter and that he may be absolved from any liability for prosecution or any other action in law in the capacity of licensee of the Cinema in the event of any illegal act or offence being committed by others in the Cinema premises. On behalf of respondent No. 2 it was contended that the impugned order was violative of principles of natural justice inasmuch as no notice or hearing had been given to the partnership firm before the order was passed. It had also been submitted on behalf Of the appellants (i) that even when the licence granted by State Government had been shown as the licensee and there is no mention at all of the partner or its partners, it did not show that he had any authority in law to conduct such exhibition of films; (ii) that the licensing authorities had no jurisdiction under the Act or the Rules to make such an order. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The power of general superintendence and control over all revenue courts vested in the Board under Section 9 of the Land Revenue Act is both administrative as well judicial powers. The appellant, a newspaper employee of the 1st respondent engaged in the production or publication of the said law reports were published by the Ist respondent. The first respondent submitted its written statement in October 1981 inter alia contending that it was not running a newspaper establishment and publications published by it were not the newspapers as defined in the Act and therefore the order made by the Central Government on the basis of the recommendations of Justice Palekar Tribunal was unsustainable by its judgment dated 22nd April, 1983. The High Court accepted the plea of the Ist Respondent and declared that the law reports did not carry any news and that the public was not interested in them. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The law reports published by tho Ist respondent are newspapers and the employees employed by the first respondent in their production or publications of the same law reports should be extended the benefit of the orders passed by the State Government on its basis. [782A] 1.2 The law Reports which are being published by an employer in their own interest vie with each other to publish the judgments of the Supreme Court or of the High Courts as early as possible in their law reports which are published periodically either weekly, fortnightly or monthly. Hence it is difficult to agree with the submission made on behalf of the first Respondent that the Law Reports do not carry out any news or that the Public is not interested In them. [783E] 1:3 The law report which are generally used in order to get reports of recent events which have taken place in the Supreme court or in the High Court Courts which are public bodies and these are matters in which the public is interested. [784G H; 784A] 2.1 In the instant case, the publication of these items by itself may not occupy a substantial part of a law report to make it a newspaper which may after some time cease to be a newspaper and become a book of reference. The publication of such items by themselves may not occupying a substantial portion of a Law report to making it a public newspaper, the publications of recent judgments itself is sufficient to make a law reports a newspaper. [ 784A B] 2:2 In the present days nothing prevents any educated individual taking interest in such publications and the news themselves being of interest to such persons. 1967 Punjab and Haryana 193 that the Gazette of India which was the official publication of all kinds of news and information was a newspaper within the meaning of section 2(b) of the Working Journalists (Conditions of Service) and Miscellaneous Provisions Act, 1955 and that it is not essential for a newspaper to conform strictly to the usual pattern of a daily or weekly newspaper or a magazine containing news which members of the public ordinarily read in order To get reports from recent events, comments on them etc. are sufficient to making a law Report a newspaper, which may thereafter after some sometime cease to he a newspaper; become a Book of reference and hence even if it is possible to have two opinions on the construction of the provisions of the Act the one which advances the object of the legislation and is in favour of the employees for whose benefit the Act is passed has to be accepted. [781C D] 2 :3 The expression `newspaper ' as defined under the Act includes not merely `public news ' but also `comments on public news '. Every law report contains the editorial note at the commencement of the decisions printed therein and also comments on some of the recent decisions. Though the publication publication of those items by it itself may be not occupy any substantial part, of alaw report to made it a paper which may later cease to have been a newspaper but become a ' book of Reference.

The appellant was a monthly tenant of the suit premises since about 2nd February, 1965. On or about 9th of February,1965 a fresh document of that date was executed and it is alleged that the licensor gave and granted his 'leave and licence ' to the licensee to use and occupy the said premises for the purpose of carrying out his business of workshop for a period of five years and whereas the licensor had agreed to allow him to occupy and use the said property for the purposes of carrying on his business. The appellant was also described as the licensee ' and the recitals therein recite that the licensee was seized and possessed of and was otherwise well entitled as the monthly tenant. The respondent filed a suit against the appellant and obtained a decree. It was alleged that this agreement was entered into between the parties since the respondent wanted to charge more rent or mesne profits. This agreement was in writing and this was for a term of five year, i.e., from 1st September 1965 to 31st August 1970. The main contention involved in this appeal is whether the appellant was the tenant or a licensee? The answer would be dependent upon the construction of the document. It is necessary, therefore, to refer to the said agreement in little detail. The agreement is described as an agreement of 'leaves and licence" entered into on between the respondent on the one hand and the appellant on the other wherein the respondent had been described as licensee and the terms recite therein reciting that the lessor was seized. It also alleged that it was agreed by the licensee that if he commits any default of any terms and conditions or fails to pay the compensation for two months or if the licensee at any time puts up false or adverse claim of tenancy or sub tenancy the licensor shall be entitled to terminate the agreement and cancel and revoke and withdraw the leave and licence granted earlier and shall be entitle to take possession forthwith of the said Premises. The trial Judge in the instant case passed a decree in ejectment petition filed by the respondent and ordered the appellant to vacate the premises before 31st January, 1975. The High Court allowed the revision on the ground that there was no subsisting agreement for licence on the 1st February 1973 as there was nothing on record to show that after 31st March 1966 the leaveand licence agreement between the two parties was renewed or any fresh agreement was enter into. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: The appellant had been carrying on business for some time, and it was a licensee and not a sub tenant. [2181 E] In order to go back to the findings of the trial Judge of the Court of Small Causes and the learned Single Judge of that High Court found that the appellant had failed to prove that he was a subtenant of the respondent, and the trial court had taken one view which is a possible and plausible view merely because another view was attractive, the High Court should not interfere and would be in error in interfering with the finding of the Trial Court or interfering under Article 227 of the Constitution over such decision. [2281 E F] In the instant appeal it was not shown that after 1st March, 1966 the lease and licence agreement were renewed or a fresh agreement entered into. The question whether the respondent was a tenant or licensee was negatived by the Small Causes Court, Bombay. The finding of fact recorded by this Court in Errington vs Erringtrington, ; , is remanded back to that High court for a fresh decision keeping in view the decision of this Court In re: D.H.

The respondent was a resident of the former Dholpur State and the dispute which led to the suit related to a time before the merger of Dholpur. The case of the respondent was that in 1947 certain commodities including chuni with which appeal No. 887 was concerned could only be exported from the former State on export permits issued by the customs department of the said State. It was also the practice in that State that when permits for export were issued, export duties had to be paid in advance though the actual export was made later. Consequently in June 1947 the respondent applied for and was granted a permit for export of 15,000 maunds of chuni, and in connection therewith he deposited Rs. 30,000/as export duty in advance. The suits were resisted by the State on various grounds; but it was contended that in view of article 295(2) of the Constitution the State of Rajasthan was bound by the obligation of the latter State of Dhol purpur State. Held: (i) that the covenant in the agreement continued to be in force in the State concerned subject always to this that if the new State passed any law repealing the old law which would affect the liability or even otherwise that law would prevail and the liability may disappear provided the new law is within the competence of the State legislature and does not transgress the constitutional limitations after the Constitution came into force. (ii)that there was recognition of liability by the new sovereign throughout this process and under the circumstances the suit was main tainable against the Part B State of Madhya Pradesh in view Of article 295 of the Covenant and similar provisions which were always made throughout this period. The fact that the old laws continued for the time being by Rajasthan Ordinance No. 1 of 1950 did not affect the recognition of such an agreement and which clearly provided for excise duties. Such a law was therefore valid. (iii)that the new Sovereign throughout this country was liable under article 295 (2) to meet the liabilities of all old States which eventually were included in it subject always always to that if that new State passing any law amending the old Act which would effect the liability, or even other otherwise, provided the law so made was within the competency of the new state and after the constitution came into operation it did not transgress its constitutional limitations. (iv)that article VI of the covenant could not be availed of by the subjects of the old State as it was just before January 26, 1950 but also the old States who came to be merged in the United State of Rajore as it then stood. The new sovereign had no recognition of the rights of the subjects and undertook the liability if any, of the existing States. (v)that even assuming that there was some doubt about the new Government undertaking the liabilities could not in accordance with the decision in the Daltia Dadri Cement Co. case. [182 D] (vi)The expression "Government of the corresponding Indian State" used in article 295 would mean only the United state of Rajasthan as it stood before January 1, 1950 and also the new States which ultimately were included into it subject to this modification that reference therein to the Ruler or Government of that State shall be construed as a reference to the Rajpramukh or, as the case may be, to the Government of Rajasthan.

No material has been placed before the Court to arrive at a definite finding in the present case whether 'mahimai ' was a deduction or not depends upon whether 'Mahimi ' was the trade allowance, within the meaning of section14 of the .

The appellants were convicted and sentenced to death by the Sessions Judge. The High Court confirmed their convictions but reduced the sentence of imprisonment to transportation for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended that section 377 of the Code of Criminal Procedure did not abrogate or modify that provision. HELD : (i) There is no evidence of any prior meeting. At bottom it is a question of fact in every case and however similar the circumstances, facts in one case cannot be used as a precedent to determine the conclusion on the facts in another. All that is necessary is either to have direct proof of prior concert or proof of circumstances which necessarily lead to that inference, or, as we prefer to put it in the time honoured way, "the incriminating facts must be incompatible with the innocence of the accused and incapable of explanation on any other reasonable hypothesis". [1097 F G] (ii) The fact that the appellants were also there but no evidence was adduced to show that they ran away together as a body or that they met afterwards. There is nothing to indicate that they run away together. It is not enough, as in the latter Privy Council case, to have the same intention independently of each other, e.g., the intention to rescue another and if necessary to kill those who oppose. In the present case there was no evidence from which a common intention embracing him can legitimately be deduced. [1099 C D] (iii) The facts disclosed do not warrant an inference of common intention in Pandurang 's case. There was evidence that all the three lived together and that one was a younger brother and the other a tenant of the appellant in question. There were no evidence to show any prior concert, or proof thereof. [1199 C] (iv) The absence of the names in the report is not of much consequence in this case especially as the names were disclosed in full at the time of the inquest. The doctor was recalled by the High Court and he gave some sort of explanation about postmortem stains on the body which we do not think is satisfactory, but the utmost this shows is that no stick blows were found on the bodies and that there was nothing to show them ran away with as a Body or that their Lordships did. There are no evidence in any prior meetings. At the bottom it was a question Of fact in each case and therefore similar the circumstance, facts of one case could not be used for determining a conclusion of fact In another case it cannot be said that there had once been a dacoity at Ramchander 's house and that he suspected "the "accused" and reported them to the police who arrested them but nothing came of it. There has been no evidence that they did ran away along with the deceased.

The respondents filed a suit in the Subordinate Court of Sub Judge, being original suit No. 2 of 1964 on 10th January, 1964. The deceased had filled a proposal for insurance Rs. 50,000 on 27th December, 1960. There was medical examination by the doctor on the life of the deceased on 27 12 1960. The appellant had issued two cheques for Rs. 300 and Rs. 220 respectively in favour of the appellant as first premium. cheque for Rs 1 herein, wrote to the appellant intimating the death of the said deceased and demanded payment of Rs. 2,000/ in full. It was further alleged that the said two cheques were encashed and the appellant had duly appropriated the amount and credited in the accounts towards the premium payable by the deceased. The Divisional Manager, Masulipatam Branch, denied liability on behalf of the Corporation on 28th January 1961. A report described as "All the Friend 's report" was duly sent to the Appellant with regard to that proposal; and all the preliminaries were completed and it was further stated that the deceased was assured and told by the local agent and the Field officer of the corporation that the payment of the first premium would amount to acceptance of the proposal and advised the deceased to pay the first premiums in full,. It is alleged that with full knowledge of the completion of all the three preliminsaries, the Corporation had encashed the cheques issued towards the first insurance and therefore it was the case of the plaintiffs respondents that the encashment of the cheques amounted in those circumstances in law to an acceptance of proposal of the respondent Corporation. The Trial Court held that there was no concluded contract between the deceased and the Corporation and that the insurance contracted commenced on 11th January. 1961 being the date of receipt of the balance towards premium by the Corporation. It also noted that it was significant that the case set out in the plaint and the basis of the claim made in the notices sent to it was not that the proposal was as a matter of fact accepted by the Divisional Manager on the other hand, claim was that it should be deemed to have been accepted. Considering the evidence and the averments, the Trial Court came to the conclusion that there were no concluded valid insurance contract between them and the respondent corporation. The High Court accordingly dismissed the suit. In this appeal by certificate, it was contended for the appellant Corporation that the plea that Divisional Manager was the only authority to accept had not been categorically taken in the written statement filed on behalf or of the respondents. It would be incorrect to say that the allegation that there is assurance on behalf the field officer and local agent to the deceased that the payments of first premium were not accepted by them cannot also be accepted firstly because factually it was proved and secondly because there was nothing to show that such acceptance was made, that did not alter the position as under the rules the payment could never amount to the acceptance of a proposal if the proposal is not otherwise accepted. It has been categorically stated in the pleadings that there Was assurance on the part of the field officers and local agents to the respondent that the amount would be transferred into the first Premium Account after the proposal had been accepted and the risk covered. The allegation that the appellant cashed the above two cheques and appropriated the amounts and credited these in the account towards premium payable for the proposal were false. It could not be said that there had been a concluded contract of insurance between the respondent and the corporation, was untenable, according to the plaintiffs. It had also been categorically denied that the acceptance was not on behalf by the respondents or that the alleged assurance if any valid under law. The allegations in the suit that there wag assurance on their part was not true nor the alleged assurances if any, valid under Law.

The plaintiffs applied for an interim injunction restraining the Bank of India Ltd. from taking any steps in pursuance of a letter of credit opened in favour of M/s V/O Tractors Export, Moscow, the second defendant. The suit was dismissed by the trial court and the High Court set aside that order. Against this order an appeal was preferred to this Court with certificate granted by the High court under article 133(1)(a) and (b). HELD: An order passed by the 'High Court in appeal which does not finally dispose of a suit or proceeding and leave the rights and obligations of the parties for determination in the suit or proceedings from which appeal has arisen, is not final within the meaning of section 109(a) of the Code of Civil Procedure. [766 F] In the present case no issue had been decided and it was not contended that the order of the High ' Court amounts to a judgment or decree. The expression "final order" in article 133 (1) means an order which finally determines the points in dispute and brings the case to an end. The test of finality, according to the court, is whether the order finally disposes of the rights of the party, and not whether the 'order decides an important point or even a vital issue in the case. [700 G H] In this case no question had been framed as to the maintainability of the claim for execution of a decree under appeal. The order refusing to grant an interim relief did not determine the rights, obligations and obligations. The proceeding instituted on the complaint was not part of or incidental to the proceeding for an enquiry whether a complaint should be filed. [601 B] In view of the decision in Mohanlal Maganlal Thakkar vs State of Gujarat, ; , it is clear that an order passed in appeal by the Bombay High Court in Appeal No. 25/68 dated April 12, 1968 which does no finally dispose or disposes of a claim or proceeding from which appeals has arisen is not a final order within the contemplation of article 133 of the Constitution.

The petitioners, who were engaged in the manufacture of dyeing and selling yarn to their customers, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the assessable value of the processed fabric at the factory gate. The High Court dismissed the petition. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (i) Rule 174 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 enjoins that when goods owned by one person are manufactured by another the information is required relating to the price at which the said manufacturer is selling the said goods and the person so authorised agrees to discharge all the liabil ities under the Act and the rules made thereunder; (ii) Rule 173 of the Rules enjoins that where goods owned in by one persons are manufactured, the information was required relating t o the price on which the goods were sold must be the value of such grey cloth or fabric plus the value or of the job work done plus manufac turing profit and expenses. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The price at the time when the goods owned are manufactured is the value at which a person who is selling them must be his value. If the trader, who entrusts cotton or man made fabric to the processor for processing on job work basis, would give a declaration to the operator as to what would be the price of the grey cloth Or fabric plus value of that job work performed plus manuufac tioned profit and expenditure. [346G H] 2. The prices at which he is selling his goods must be taken by the Excise authorities as the assessable valuation of the processing fabric and excise duty would be charged to the applicant on that basis provided that the declaration as to the value in which he would be selling the processed goods in the market, would include only the price or deemed price at Which the processed fabrics would leave the processor 's factory plus his profit. [347A B] 3. The cost and charges plus profit, but not any other subsequent profit or expenses. It is necessary to include the processor "s expenses, costs and charges, plus profit. But it is not necessary to mention the trader 's profits who gets the fabrics processed, because those would be post manufacturing profits.

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on June 1, 1963 by the Panchayat Samiti. On March 14, 1975 a resolution was passed by respondent 3 regularising the post of Head Clerk. The appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in January 1974 or the further fact that he was appointed to the post on April 1, 1975 cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13, 1973 when the Amending Act came into force. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The appellant 's appointment to the posts of Head Clerks being without the authority of law, the Government was not bound to absorb him in the post as of a Head clerk. He was appointed lawfully to the Post of a Clerk and that is the post in which the Government has absorbed him. [737B] (2) The appointment of the appellant to the said post being without authority of Law, the government was not entitled to absorb himself in the posts or to make appointments to the Panchayat. [750C D] (3) The fact that the appellant was promotion as a head clerk on an Ad hoc basis cannot improve the position for his simple reason because he had been appointed lawfully and that was the post which the Govern ment has absorbed, cannot improve their position for this simple reason. [751E F] (4) The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, what is relevant for our purpose is not whether the appellant is entitled to be consider ed for promotion but, whether the Panchayat had the right to appoint him to the office of Head clerk on the date on which it purported to do so. Clearly, it had fortified that right on June 13 1973. It could not, therefore, have appointed the appellant as a Headmaster, as it purported merely to do, in January, 1974 on an ex hoc basis or in April 1975 on a regular basis.

The appellants filed a suit claiming that the property in dispute belonged to the Math Sauna or the deity Sri Thakur, and that Mahant Sadashiva Yati was in possession thereof as Mahant and Sarbarakar of the deity. The suit was contested by the first defendant, Kedar Nath Chaubey, also referred to as Uma Shankar Yati. He claimed that he was the chela of Mahant Shivshanker Yati and the Amauli properties had passed to him under a will executed by the Mahant. The trial court decreed the suit but included a finding in his judgment that Sadashiv Yati had not been a regularly constituted Mahant of Math Saa and Sarbakar of deity, and the income derived therefrom was not liable to tax. The High Court allowed both the appeals by its judgment and decree dated April 21, 1969. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that where a nucleus of dedicated property exists, the acquisition of additional property should be attributed to the application of the nuclean and must, therefore, be regarded as property belonging to the math or deity. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The fund from which the Amaiuli properties were acquired constituted the personal property of Mahant Sheo Shankar Yatati and do not form part of the properties of the Math or of the temple. [663 C] 2.1 There is reason to believe that Mohant Shivbaran Yati, Mohant, Shivpher Yati & Mahant Shiv Shankar Yuther Shankar Yayati were not celibates and had been grihasthas, and were entitled to possess, enjoy and acquire personal property. The evidence disclosed that Mahant Shivphar Yati who owned three private properties in village Amauli in 1921 employed it for the purchase of the Amaul properties. Mahant Shivshhankar Yati executed a will in 1956 and it appears beyond dispute that by virtue of this will the Amaiii properties devolved on Uma ShankarYati. It is pointed out before us that in assessment proceedings under the U. P. Agriculture Income Tax Act 1948, the Amaoli properties were described by Mahant Shiv Shivshankar Yatti as properties of Math and therefore a claim to exemption from the levy was made. The appellants had also inherited the personal properties of Mahant Sadasiva Yatri. [665 C] 3.2 In assessment proceedings U.P. Agriculture income Tax Act, 1948,the Amauli property were described in the name of Mahant Sri Shiv ShankarYatti and not that of the math nor the deity, but small parcels of these properties were transferred by Mahant Sheo Shiv Shankar Yadav from time to time, and none of those transfers was challenged by the appellants in the present suit. It was pointed out that in assessing proceedings under U. O.XXI of Article 133 of the Constitution, the Thai properties were mentioned by Mahant Sri Ram Shivs Shankar Yanti. The Mahants and members of Math, Sauna belonged to Dharmanikhan Yati but none of these transfers was questioned by the plaintiffs in the suit.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of 24 standard acres and 15 3/4 units in the village of Raikot in 1949. Their father Sardar Nand Singh made an application for consolidation of his lands with those of the appellants in the villages. During the pendency of this application he died and after his death, the application was continued by the appellants. The Assistant Custodian General cancelled the allotment on the ground that no land was available in the Village Raikot. On appeal the Additional Custodian General set aside the order cancelling the allotment of land in favour of the appellant. The High Court held that the powers of the Custodian General to deal with matters of this kind have been taken away by the and that these powers now vest in another authority and there is no provision for continuing the pro ceedings which had been commenced under the but had not been concluded. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lants that (i) the Custodian 's power to deal With matters of allotment or cancellation of allotment of evacuee property has been taken over by virtue of section 19(1) of the 1954 Act and therefore they would be entitled to the benefits conferred by this section provided they satisfied all other requirements of this section, express or implied; (ii) there is nothing on record to show that a managing officer was appointed with respect to the Raikot properties acquired under the notification dated March 24, 1955. HELD: (i)(a) The Custodian 'had the power to allot any property to a person or to cancel an allotment existing in favour Of a person rests on the fact that the property vests in him. But the consequence of the publication of the notification by the Central Government under section 12(1), with respect, to any property or a class of property would be to divest the Custodian completely of his right in the property flowing from section 8 of the , and vest that property in the Central Govern ment. No provision was however pointed out to us in either of these Acts whereunder despite the Vesting of the property in tho Central Government the Custodian was empowered to dealwith it. [337 C D] (b) The appellants had lost their possession before the publication. Of this notification. Even assuming that the order of the custodian cancelling the allotments in their favour was erroneous there will be no difference in the result because what is essential is the facts of holding and possession of the land on the date of the Notification. The Uttar Pradesh Public Service Commission had undertaken the recruitment to the post of Upper Basic Shiksha Adhikari (Women) District Inspectress of Girls Schools in Uttar Pradesh Educational Service Junior Scale (Women 's Branch) The advertisement inviting applications from eligible candidates was published on May 5, 1985 and a corrigendum was published. The recruitment examination was in two stages written and interview/personality test. After the written examina tion was over, on the basis of the results thereof success ful candidates upto a base limit have to be called to be interviewed. On account of improper feeding into the comput er some of the candidates who had better performance in the written examination were not called and candidates securing lesser marks in the interview were not only called for interview but were also finally selected. When this position was known and upon an inquiry was factually estab lished, the Public Service Com mission decided to cancel the entire recruitment examination and asked for re holding of it. The High Court upheld the action of the Public Services Commission and dismissed the writ petitions. In these appeals by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that when no defect was pointed out in regard to the written exami nation and the sole objection was confined to exclusion of a group of successful candidates in the oral examination from the interview, there was no justification for cancelling the written part of the recruitment examina t tion. On the other hand, it is contended on their behalf that when there was a defect pointed out, there could be no justification in cancelling the re spondents 's written part and asking for a fresh interview of all eligible candidates on the ground that there was an error apparent on the face of record. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. When no defect is pointed out In regard to an written examination and the only objection was restricted to exclusion, of a Group of successful candidate in the viva voce test from the interviewed interview, it could have been appropriately met by setting aside the recruitment and asking of a fresh exami nal of all candidates on tho basis of written examination. [126E] 2. When there is no defect pointed in regardto the written re quirement and the main objection was confine to exclusion. The situation could have be appropriately met By setting aside of the selection and asking the for a new interview of those who on the basi sation of the written and the freshly held interview became eligible for selection.

The appellant brought the suit on the allegation that there was one Shiromani Nirankari Dera at Patiala, that this institution had two branches one at Landeke in Moga Tehsil and the other at Nanga Kheri in the erstwhile Patiala State. The prayer in the plaint was for recovery of possession of the Dera and the properties attached to it. Som Dass, the defendant, contended that the Dhoh at Landake was an independent Dera, that he was in possession of those properties as its lawfully appointed mahant, that the appellant had no right to recover possession of these properties of the dera and entitled to manage the properties of Dera. The trial court decreed the suit. In appeal by the defendant the decree was reversed. Against this decree an appeal was preferred by the appellant to the High Court. While the appeal was pending in the High court, Som Dass died on 13 10 1970. No application was made by the appel lant to bring on record his legal representatives within the period prescribed. An application was filed on 1 2 1971 by the plaintiff stating that Som Dass had died on 26 11 1970 leaving behind him Shiam Dass as his Chela and for impleading him, that Som Das, the respondent, who was the mahant of the said Dera should be impleaded as a party under Order 22, r. 10, of the Civil Procedure Code against the person upon whom the interest had devolved, and that the appe lant did not know about the death of Som Dass at the time he died. The High Court held that after the death Of Som Dass Shiam Das, Shiam Chand as his chela "inherited the sum total of the rights which earlier vested in Som Dass and when a controversy is raised about such rights, then the appellant was bound to bring the suit for the recovery of posses sion of the properties. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the respondent that there were no devolution of the interest in the subject matter of the suit, since there was no certainty as to the person who would be elected as mahant to succeed him. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The devolution of interest in a subject matter is taken place when Shiam Ram Dass was elected as Mahants of the temple after the demise of Som Das Dass. Som Das was sued in his capacity as a person who claimed (though illegally according to the appellant) as mahants of Dhogh and Som Dass was sued and as it was in the same representative capacity that the appeal is sought to be continued against Shiam Lal, Order 22 rule 10 would not be attracted. [489C] 2. The suit against Som Dass is not in his personal capacity but in his capacities as de facto mahant. In other words, the suit was for possession and management of the Eera and its properties and it devolved upon shiam Dass by virtue of his election as ma ties subsequent to the death. [490E F] 3. The word 'interest ' which is mentioned in this rule means interest in property i.e., the subject matters of the main suit and the interest is the interest of the person, who is the party to the suit.[490G H] 4. devolution of a interest in an estate cannot be brought to an end merely because the interest or of a party in the matter of suit has devolved upon another during the pendency of the litigation but that suit may be continued on the person acquiring the interest with the leave of the Court. When a suit is brought by or against a person in a representative capacity and there is a devolution of his interest, the rule that has to be applied is Order 22 Rule 10 and not rule 3 or 4, whether the devolution takes place as a consequence of death or for any other reason.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Andhra Pradesh State Electricity Board. In 1983, a new political party called Telugu Desam was swept to power. It assumed office on January 9, 1983. On February 8, 1983 an Order (G.O. Ms. No. 36) was issued by the Government of Andhra Pradesh stating that it had decided to reduce the age of superannuation of all Government employees, other than in the last Grade Service from 58 to 58 years. The case of the petitioners as laid in the writ petitions is that there was no basis at all for reducing the age Of retirement from 58 and that the age was increased from 55 to 58 by the State Government by a notification dated October 29, 1979 and nothing had happened since then to justify reduction of the age. The petitioners contended that the provisions of the Ordinance whereby the ageof retirement is reduced from 58 years to 55 is arbitrary and irrational and violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution for the following reasons: (a) The decision to reduce age of retirement from 55 is unconstitutional because it is arbitrary, irrational and unconnected with the object which it seeks to achieve. In this connection, the first ground of challenge to the reduction of age of retire ment is that the One man Pay Revision Commission appointed by the Andhra pradesh Government had recommended that the case of retirement should be increased from 58, that the said recommendation was accepted by the state Government and consequently, the age for retirement was raised to 58 with effect from October 29 l9 79. (b) The recommendations of the Third Central Pay Commission that the date of birth of the employees should be changed from 55 and that it was the duty of the State within the limits of its economic capacity and development to make effective provision to solve the unemployment problem. (c) The recommendation of the Second Central Pay Commis sion that the retirement age of the retired employees should he increased from55 to 58 is not accepted by Government initially because, it felt that raising the age would reduce employment opportunities in the immediate future. For these reasons, the Commission recommended that a certain minimum age be raised from 55 years to 58, and that this was done by the petitioners in 1979 by increasing the age from 55, that it should take effect from the afternoon of the last day of the month in which the employee attains the age 56 years. (d) The question as regards the age is a pure question of Governmental policy affording no cause of action to the petitioners to file the writ petition. It is stated in that affidavit that the question of the ages of retirement was not referred to the Commission and that, the decision which the Government took later to increase the age should be taken by it within one month of the assumption of office by it cannot justify the conclusion that lt the decision is arbitrary because it overlooks the advance made in longevity, fixation of retirement age at 58 is also not likely to sustain the charge of arbitrariness. The recommendation regarding increasing the date was accepted on October 29. 979 and it was later, in October 1979 that the Government decided on its own to increase its age of retired employees from 55to 58 years, that this recommendation was made by the Commission almost in their entirety, it did not accept its recommendations that the time of retirement would reduceemployment opportunities in public services of the state; (e) The report of the Commission has therefore to be kept out of consideration in so far as the question regarding the age and retirement is concerned and no argument can be founded on the fact that the view of the Commisisoner was ignored or that nothing had been happened since the date when the report to justify a departure from it. (f) The Report of the Commissioner has therefore, to be retained out of the consideration in accordance with the recommendations made by him.

The appellants are a registered dealer in the State of Haryana. He purchased certain raw materials in the state without paying tax thereon, in view of the provision contained in section 24 of the Haryana Sales Tax Act, 1973. The assessee was not liable to pay the purchase tax on the raw materials imposed under section 9(1) of the Act. This claim has been rejected by the taxing authorities and the High Court and hence these appeals. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The purchases of raw materials by the assessees are goods on the sales of which tax is leviable under the Act though the assessees were exempt from payment of such tax by reason of section 24(1). [351G] 2. The definition also excludes from its purview "the sale proceeds of goods on which purchase tax is levied under this Act" and "the purchase value of any goods on tho sales of Which tax is payable under this act". There can be no dispute that a tax is impos ed under the statute on the goods in question when they are sold by a dealer and, indeed, the assessees would have had to pay tax on them. But let us examine what the position would be if we hold, as con tended by Shri Gupta, that the effect of the decision is that the words "or despatches the manufactured goods to a place outside the State in any manner otherwise than by way of sale in the course of inter State trade or commerce" in section 9 (1)(b) should be deemed to have been deleted from the statute. This definition includes within the definition of 'turnover ' the purchase value o f goods liable to tax under section 8 but, the goods presently in question are not laible to tax u/s 9(i) or section 6 or section 24 (3). [353C D] 3. The words "disposes of" used in clause (a)(ii) later, clause (b) also includes cases of despatches by a registered dealers of the manufactured candi dates outside the territory of India within the meaning of sub section (1)of section 5 of the Central Sales Tax. [353F] 4.

The appellants were registered dealers under the Indian Partnership Act. In their return of turnover for the period from April 1, 1954 to March 31, 1955 they claimed exemption from sales tax in respect of sales of cotton of the total value of Rs. 68,493 2 6 and sales of castor oil of the value of RS. 6,47,509 1 6 on the ground that these sales were oil FOB contracts under which they continued to be the owners of the goods till the goods had crossed the customs barrier and thus entered the export stream and so no tax was realisable on these sales in view of the provisions of article 286(1)(b). The Sales Tax Officer rejected this claim for exemption and assessed them to sales tax on a taxable turnover including those sales. He also assessed them as purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act on their purchase of cast or oil which they later sold for the sum of Rs, 68,490 2 6 on their purchases of castar oil of total value Rs. 647,059 1 6 and sale of castr oil of Rs 6, 47,510 1 6. The appellants contended that the goods remained the sellers ' property till these crossed the Customs barrier and therefore they entered the exported stream and thus no tax could be realisable under article 286 (1)(a) of Constitution. Held:(i) The words " a person" in section 10 (b) are not intended to be used as a synonymously defined but must be construed with reference to the context in which it is used. In the present case the intention declared has not been carried out and the scheme of the Legislature clearly is that where the intention as declared has neither been carried 'out, purchase tax should be levied. The scheme of section 10 shows that where a intention as to declare had not been carrying out purchase tax could not be held to have commenced till at least the ship carrying the goods has left the port, though it may in some contexts be more correct to say that it does not commence until the ship has passed beyond the territorial waters. The legislature insisted that the certificate should declare the goods purchased were intended for being despatched by him or by a registered dealer to whom he sells the goods outside the State of Bombay. In other words, if at the time a declaration of intention is made in the certificate the purchasing dealer had the intention of as stated and ultimately he sells to a person who is not a registereddealer for despatch of the ' goods outside tho State of Madras, the purchasing dealers may not be liable for having made a false declaration. Even though he has not made a untrue declaration of his intention, the fact remains that the intention so declared has no been carried on. The intention declared had not not been complied with. (ii)The scheme of sections 8 and 10 justifies the conclusion that the Legislature was anxious to secure that the declaration as regards intention of the parties being despatched outside the state of Bombay should be carried out by despatch by " a registered dealers" to whom they sells the 'goods. If such despatch outside the country of Bombay is by a person to whom the certifying dealer has sold the goods but who isnot a registered owner, the certificate has not not be complied with and it will be in our opinion unreasonable to think that though the Legislature insisted that certificate should declaring the goods purchase were intended to have been despatched by some person who was not a Registered dealer for despatch outside tho state of Madras , the legislature would be content to accept actual despatch outside tile State of Delhi by one who is a not a " registered dealer" as sufficient.

The respondent husband married the appellant (wife) as a second wife, way back in 1956 and a few years later had a son by her. 15 The initial warm vanished and the jealousies of a triangular situation erupted marring mutual affection. The respondent divorced the appellant around July 1962. A suit relating to a flat in which the husband had housed the wife resulted in a consent decree which also settled the marital disputes. For instance, it recited that this respondent had transferred the suit premises, namely, a flat to the appellant and also the shares of the Cooperative Housing Society which built the flat concerned. There was a clause in the compromise: G The appellant declares that she has now no claim or right whatsoever against the defendant or against the estate and the properties of the defendant. " And another term in the settlement was that the appellant had by virtue of the compromise become the absolute owner of the flat and various deposits in respect of the said flat made with the cooperative housing society. 78 For some time there was flickering improvement in the relations between the quondum husband and the quundum wife and they lived together. Thereafter again they separated became entranged. The appellant finding herself in financial straits and unable to maintain herself, moved the magistrate under section 125 of the Criminal Procedure Code 1973 for a monthly allowance for the maintenance of herself and her child. She proceeded on the footing that she was still a wife while the respondent rejected this status and asserted that she had been a divorcee. The Magistrate who tried the petition for maintenance held that the appel lant was a subsisting wife and awarded monthly maintenance of Rs. 300/ for the son and Rs. 400/ for her mother for their subsistence taking due note of the fact that the cost of living in Bombay, where the parties lived, was high, and that the respondent had provided residential accommodation to the appellanant. This order was challenged before the Sessions Judge by the aggrieved husband who on a strange view of the law that the court under section 127 had no jurisdic tion to consider whether the applicant was a wife, dismissed the petition in allowance of the appeal. The High Court rejected the revision petition and summarily dismissed a revision petition. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Courts below had surprisingly forgotten the plain provision in the Explanation (b) to section 125(1) of the Code which reads: "wife ' includes a woman who has been divorced by or has obtained a divorce from her husband and has not remarried. On this foundation he urged that accepting the contention of the respondent that the wife was still entitled to an allowance, his client was still enti tled to an allowances. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The basic condition of neglect to maintain is satisfied. In the normal course, an order for maintenance must follow, the quantum having been determined by the learned Magistrate at the trial level. 79 However, Shri Sanghi, appearing for the respondent sought sustain ing the order in his favour on three grounds (1) that there must be proof of neglect of to maintain attract section 125 and his third contention was that there was a settlement by consent decree in 1962 whereby the mehar money had been paid and all claims adjusted, and so no claim for maintenance could survive. The crucial question is whether the liability to pay maintenance had ceased on account of the payment of mehar, it is section 127(3)(b) absolution from this obligation under section125 towards a divorced wife except on proof of payment of a sum stipulated by customary or personal law whose quantum is more or less sufficient to do duty for maintenance allowance.

The appellant, a dealer in liquor shop, had bid for Rs.11,900 (Rupees eleven thousands only) per month Dak in an auction of Beni Country liquor shop held on 27.3.88 and he as given the shop of Beni country liquor but after signing in Bandobasti Register he did not deposit dak amount. The name of Shri Raghu Nath Thakur S/o Late Gorakh Nath Village Repura, P.S. Pusa, Distt. Samastipur was placed in the black list for future under the orders passed by the Collector, Samasti. This order was passed pursuant to the order of the Collector. The letter dated 25th March, 1988 stated that no notice had been given to the appellant of the proposal of black listing the appellant. It was contended on behalf of the State Government that there was no requirement in the rule of giving any prior notice before black listing any person. In so far as the contention that there is no requirement specifically of giving a prior notice is concerned, the respondent was right. But it was an implied principle of the rule that any order having civil consequence should be passed only after following the principles of natural justice. It has to be realised that black listing every person in respect of business ventures has civil consequence for the future business of the person concerned in any event. Even if the rules do not express so, it is an elementary principle of natural Justice that parties affected by any order should have right of being heard and making representations against the order. In this view of the matter, the last portion of the order in so far it directs black listing of the appellant in respect thereof cannot be sustained in law.

The property which was the subject matter of the lease under exhibit P 1 belonged to several co owners. The rent for the premises was Rs. 150 per month. The second lease deed (Ext. P 2) dated 3 10 1947 and related to Door No. 534/66, the Court on a perusal of the sale deed dated 30 7 53 filed by the LIC before it came to the conclusion that the buildings on the land leased under exhibit PW 1 had also been conveyed to the LIC and that the LIC was entitled to seek fixation of fair rent in respect of this premises also. 87 of 72 by a common judgment dated 23 10 1972, the contention urged on behalf of the tenants was that since the subject materi als of the suit were only a vacant site, the Rent Controller had no juris diction to fix the fair rent and therefore the claim in the suit for arrears of rent based on the Rent Control Controller 's order in respect thereof had to fail. No. In view of this finding it was held that the Rent controller had no jurisdiction to entertain the application for fixation offair rent in regard to the property which had only a small piece of land and that, therefore, the claim for arrears based on Rent Control Order in respect o f the premises covered by exhibit P1 had to fall. The question before this Court was whether the order of the Court of Small Causes in the earlier rent control proceedings deciding to the contrary and fixing the fair ly rent of item 1 at Rs.994 p.m. should be completely ignored as an order passed totally without jurisdiction, although it has become final as be tween the parties? The question for consideration was whether a Rent Controller and on appeal from him, the court of Small Cause were not competent to go into the question of title in view of the decision in the first set of proceedings. Dismissing the Appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to decide whether the denial or claim is bona fide, the rent Controller may have to go through the tenant 's contentions on the issue but he is not to decide the question finally. So also, in an application under section 4, the jurisdiction of the Rent Authori ties is to determine a fair or standard rent for tho premises. It will be anomalous to hold that where an owner of property seeks to evict his tenant under section 10(2)(vii) but the Rent inves tion Controller refuses to pass the order o f eviction though satisfied about his title because the tenant had acted bona fide it would be open to the owner to seek eviction by having his title adjudicated upon in a civil court but that the owner cannot have a similar right in the matter of recovery of rent which is basically a relief for which he has to approach a civil Court. [549C D] 1.2 In order that a petition under section4 is filed, the tenant, on the language of section 4 has to decide: (1) whether the applicant is a tenant in, or landlord of, the building and (2) what the fair Rent rent of the premises should be in accordance with the provisions of the Act. It was, therefore not open to him to contend that it was not open tO the Court to go in question of the title in ques tion in view Of the decision of the first setting of proceedings; for such a suit would be barred by section 12(4) of the Tamil Nadu Estates (Abolition and Conversion into Ryotwari) Act, 1948 which ran as follows: "64 C. Finality of orders passed under this Act in respect off matters to be determined for the purposes of this Act shall, subject only to any appeal or revision provided by or under this act, be final.

The petitioner was given ample opportu nity to file his objections to the preliminary list. The respondent, who had not appeared before the Court and, therefore, could not be heard by this Court. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The combined final gradation list dated April 6, 1962, so far as category 6 is concerned, is ultra vires and illegal and that part of the notification alone must be quashed by grant of a writ in the nature of certiorari. [828B] 1.2 In view of the special circumstances of the present case, it was not necessary to go into the merits or otherwise of equation of posts which is a matter within the province of the Central Government. It was also held there (at p. 2106): "It is no doubt true that the Central Govern ment must have due regard to the princi ples enunciated by it in consultation with the States for the purpose of equation Of posts and preparation of gradation lists. It has also to give a full and fair opportuni ty to the parties affected to make their representations; and the Central Gov ernment has also, to give, a proper consideration to those representations. So long as the Central Gover nment has acted properly according to the provisions of the Act, it is not within the Province of the courts to lay down what are in the principles to be adopted for purposes of equation. That falls within the purview of the statute concerned and the authorities charged with such duty. [829E F] 1:3 The petitioner respondent was entitled to an opportunity to make a representation with regard to two points urged by him before the final gradation lists were published. As no such opportunity was furnished to the respondents with regard t he two matters, this Court is of the view that a Court cannot go into merits or other conclu sion of equation o posts which are a matter in the province. [830F] 1 :4 The petitioner had ample opportunity to do that. Hence, the principle recognised in Shankariah 's case was not applicable to such a case.

The petitioners in both these writ petitions are partnership firms carrying on business of import of rough diamonds and export of cut and polished diamonds. The Import & Export Policy for the period April 1978 to March, 1979 in para 174 of the Import & Exports Policy for a period of 12 months was made provision for grant of certain import facilities to Export Houses which were registered in accordance with the provisions of the said Policy. One of the aforesaid facilities was grant of an Additional Licence in terms of para 176 of the Policy for an amount to be calculated at one third the f.o.b. value of the exports of select products made by the Export House in the year 1977 78. The petitioners submitted application for registration as Export Houses and for grant or renewal of Export House Certificate which would have entitled them to the grant of such Additional Licence. The said applications were rejected by the authorities on the view that petitioners had failed to diversify their export of "Other products" during the year1977 78. In these writ petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution, it was contended for the petitioners that sub para (10) of para 218 of the import Policy 1988 91 arbitrarily discriminates between Export Houses who were issued Additional licences prior to April 1, 1988 and Export Houses, who were granted Additional Licences prior to March 1,1988 in as much as the conditions of eligibility for grant/ renewal of such licences under the Import and Export Policy 1978 79 were quite different from those contained in the Import& Export Policy 198891. It was further contended that under Import & export Policy 197879 Additional licences were to be given on the basis of one third of the f,o.f. 1.4.1988 and that the petitioners had been subjected to arbitrary and hostile discrimination. The respondents in their counter affidavit submitted that there is no similarity between the petitioners who have been granted Additional licences on the strength of their exports made during the period 1977 78 in accordance With the Import Policy 1978 80. It has been further contended by the respondents that under import & Export policy 1978 79 Additional Licences were to he given on 'the basis of not foreign exchange earnings from the exports actually made and the value of such additional licence is only 10 to 12% of the net Foreign Exchange earnings. The aforesaid examination shows that while in the import & export policy 1978 80, the emphasis was only on the f .o.e. value. of exports without taking into account the outgo of foreign exchange in importing the goods required for achieving the export by an Export House and Additional Licences are granted for a much larger amount at a high percentage on the ' basis of the F.O.F.R. 1988 91, the petitioners cannot claim the benefit of the same relaxation and assail the validity of sub para 10 of para 215 of the Imports & Exports policy 1988 91. It had been further submitted that under the import and Export policy 1990 79 Additional licences are to be granted on the basic basis of an 'foreign exchange earnings ' from the export actually made ' and the 'value of such ' additional licence ' is only ten to 12%. On behalf of the respondents it has been contended that there was no similarity in between the petitioner who have already been granted additional licences on their exports during that period 1977 79 in accordancewith the Import Trade & Export Scheme 1988 91 inasmuch as the condition of eligibility was quite different and that under Imports & Export policies 1978 79, Additional Licences issued to Export House which had been granted Export Houses prior to 1. 4.1988 will also be valid for import of items of spares appearing in Appendices 2,3, 5 Part A 8 and 10 of this Policy.

The appellant is a division of McDowell & Co. Ltd., which manufactures and sells fusel oil/Styrene Monomer falling under Tariff Item No. 68 of the Ist Schedule to the Act. The case of the appellant is that the said fusel Oil is a com pletely manufactured article and after completion of its manufacture, it is stored in storage tanks duly approved for this purpose. It is at this stage that the quantity of fusel oils/Stirene Moulders manufactured according to the appel lant is entered in the RG 1 Register maintained for goods manufactured by the appellant. The Tribunal held that at the time of removal, the goods were delivered from the factory in packed condition and the containers were not returnable by the buyer, there fore, the value had to be included in the assessable value. Collector of Central Excise (Appeals) upheld the order of the Assistant Collector. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appe lant that the cost of packing could be included only when the packing is either manufactured by him or is purchased by the assessee. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The cost of the containers envisaged in section 4(4)(d)(i) does not in clude within its ambit the cost to be includible under clause 4(1)(ii) of the Act, for determining the "value" in relation to the excisable goods for computing the duty payable on it. [995G H] 2. The measure of excise duty is price and not value. It has also to be borne in mind that in any event in so far as Styrene Moger Oil is concerned, the valuation of such packing would fall under section 4 (4)(D)(i). [996A B] Union of India & Ors. vs Bombay Tyre International Ltd., ; , referred to. 3. The "cost of such pack ing" referred in section 2(4) (d)(1) does no in cluding within its scope the cost for packing not incurred by the manufacturer when the pack ing is supplied by the customer and not the manufacturer. This construction of the expres sion "cost" rather than "value", the nature of other payments referred to in sub clause (ii) all these show beyond doubt that, while generally the normal price for which the goods are sold at the factory gate is to be taken as the assessable valuation, an addition thereto has to be made where, in addition to the price, the manufacturer levies a charge for the packing which is intrinsically and inevitably incidental to placing the manufactured goods on the market. It will indeed be anomalous if the cost Of an item of pack charged for from the customer is to he excluded from the assessablevalue where the packing, though durable, is returnable to the manufacturer but the cost price of such item of packing supplied by him and taken back by him is liable to be include in the deter mination. [996C D] Union Of India & ors. vs Godfrey Phillips, by the learned Attorney General. [1986] Vol. I S.C.R. 986; Union of lndia vs Godafrey Philips, ; , relied on. 4. The object and purpose of the levy, the meaning of the expression "assessable value" as interpreted in section before its amendment cou pled with the now well established position that the amend ment intended to make no change in this position, the use of the word "cost", rather than 'value", is the nature and quality of the other payments refer ed to in subsection (ii).
