The petitioner company was found guilty of an offence punishable under section 630 of the Indian Penal Code. The Magistrate convicted the petitioner company and sentenced it to pay a fine of Rs. 1000/ . On appeal, the High Court held that the provisions contained in sub section (1) of section 630 which provide for the launching of prosecution against an officer or employee of a company for wrongful possession of such property under cls. (a) and (b) of sub section(1) thereof are not attracted to the case. In the special leave petition it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the legislature never intended to include past officers and employees of a Company within the ambit of section630(1)(b) by giving a restrictive meaning to the terms 'officer or employee ' appearing in sub s.(1) against such officer or employees which must take its colour from the context in which it appears. Dismissing the special Leave Petition, ^ HELD: 1. The words 'any such property ' occurring in section 630(l)(b), relate to any property of a firm as mentioned in cl. (b). According to the plain construction, the words 'every such property" in el. (c) relate to "any property of the company as mentioned In cl. Section 630 of H 172 the Act plainly makes it an offence if an officer and employee of the Company who was permitted to use any property during his employment wrongfully withholds possession of it after the termination of his employment. By a curious process of reasoning, the Court of Calcutta in Amritlal Chum vs Devi Ranjan Jha & Anr., held that section 630 applies only to the existing officers and employee employees of the said company and not to those whose employment has been terminated. [179E F] 2. The High Court of Bombay in Amrit Lal Chum 's case did not lay down good law and was therefore right in holding that the terms "officer or servant" appearing in section 630(l) are the only construction possible. [180B C] 3. The expression "any such thing" occurring in sub sec.(1)(a) of Section 630 must be interpreted to mean not only the present officers and Employees of a ' company but also to include future officers and staff of the same company. It is also possible for such an officer, or employee after termination of the employment, to wrongfully take away possession of any such property. [181C D] 4. The construction placed by the High court on the provisions in section6 30(1), namely, that "if any officer or servant of a companies wrongfully withhold 's possession" of any property wrongfully obtained by an officer/ employee of that company during the course of his service, to which he is not entitled, and knowingly applies it to purposes other than those expressed or directed in the articles and authorised by the Act. [182D E] 5. The conclusion of the High Courts that the term "officer" or employee " appearing in cl.(b) must be construed to mean only the past officers or employees of that Company but also include past officer and employees, is not correct. [183E F; 184A B] 6. The language used by the Legislature in enacting sub section 1 of section 629 of the Act is the only interpretation possible. It would be rendered nugatory by projecting cl. There is no warrant for the construction placed on the words "any other such property". occurring in el.(b), as applicable to such property of that a company, possession of which is wrongfully obtained, by an Officer or employee, of the companies during the Course of his appointment, wrongfully retains or occupies the same after the terminated of his services.

The appellant was the founder of a temple. He had movable property of the value of Rs. 19,164/ and immovable properties of the values of Rs, 1,06,000/ and the average gross annual income as well as the average annual expenditure was Rs. 11,000. After the passing of the Bombay Public Trusts Act 1950 (No. 29 of 1950) an application under section 18 of that Act was filed by three persons who were members of a public religious trust. The word 'Buwa ' means saint. At the close of the enquiry the Assistant Charity Commissioner held the Sansthan to be a public trust and ordered its registration as a public Trust under the Act. The District Judge reversed the decision of the Charity Commissioner by his order dated October 16, 1959. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the Sansthan in question is an endowment; (2) there is absolutely no evidence of long user of the temple by the public as a matter of right; and (3) the Sanad being an ancient Royal grant is a very important piece of evidence to show that although Sakharam Maharaj, the founder, of the Temple, had already been succeeded by Guru Govindbuwa and the latter by Balkrishnabuwa, the land had been held in the year 1860 61 in the name of the Devasthan. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The expression in the recital that "you are free as the full owner thereof" does not convert the gift which is expressly in favour of the deity or Sansthan into that in favour Of an individual as private property. This Court further held that when property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol, it is a public and not a public endowment, as the persons who are entitled to worship at the shrine of the idol can only be the members of the family, and that is an ascertained group of individuals. Distinguishing the decision in Bahu Bhagwan Din vs Gir Har Saroon on the ground that the properties in that case were granted not in favour to an idol or temple but in favour thereof by one Daryao Gir who was maintaining a temple and to his heirs in perpetuity, this Court further observed: "When it is understood that the true beneficiaries of religious endowments are not the idols but the worshippers, and the purpose of the endowment is the maintenance of that worship for the benefit of worshippers, the question whether an endowment is private or public presents no difficulty. In accordance with this theory, it has been held that whenever property is dedication for the temple of a Hindu family idol it is, a private and not public endowment as the person who are enti to worship in at the Shrine of deity can only he the members members of his family, but that is a ascertained group Of individuals. [532 D] (b) The consciousness of the constituted attorney about the nature of the property which has been dealt with or managed by those in charge, the manner in which the property has long been used by the Public, the contribution of the public to all intents and purposes as a matters of right without the least interference or restriction from the temple authorities, to foster maintenance of the worship the accretion to the trust property by way of grants from the state of gifts from outsiders inconsistent with the private nature of trust, the nature, of devolution of the properties, are all important elements in determination of the question Whether a property is a private or a public Religious endowment. [525 E] (c) The appellant 's evidence, therefore, is without any force.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947 1948 and 1951 1952 by the Third Income tax Officer, C 1 Ward Bombay, at and for Rs. 2,000/ . The assessee not having paid up the assessed amount of tax the Income tax officer issued a warrant of arrest under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876 requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1955 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the said demand. The Additional Collector of Bombay issued a proclamation under section 46(2) of the Act requiring the appellant to appear in person before him on the 15th June, 1955 and explain why he was not apprehended and confine to civil prison in satisfaction Of the said certified demand. On the 16st June 1955 the second respondent issued a notice under section13 of the Indian Bombay City Revenue Act calling upon the assessee (assessee) to show cause as to why he be should not apprehended, and confined in the civil jail under the rules in force at the Presidency for the purpose of being released forthwith. The appellant contended that the provisions of the State laws which prescribe that machinery are not incorporated in section 46 (2) were void under article 13(1) of Constitution inasmuch as they infringed article 14 of the Constitution. Held, that the procedure prescribed by section 13 was not ultra vires and could not be regarded as having crept into section 46.(2). The provisions of all the State law for recovery of arrears of land revenue had been referentially incorporated in sections 46(1), 47(2), 48 and 49 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1879 in that a defaulter residing in the City of Bombay could be kept in detention for a day for every rupee of the arrears which might considerably exceed the maximum period of six months which was the period limited by the Code. The State laws prescribing procedure for recovery were not ultra rites as they were not incorporated into section 47(1).

The respondents were the trustees of a Port Trust Employees ' Union. The Trustees agreed to accept the hours of rest at fixed hours in the Alexandra Docks but at the Prince 's and Victoria Docks they kept it variable agreeing to fix it as near the middle of the duty hours as possible. The respondents accepted the hours for rest at the rate of 12 hours shift and paid overtime wages. The claim of the shore crew at theince 's & Victoria Dock was not accepted because the amount of work in the opinion of the Trustees did not justify the change. The Union contended that this division of 12 hour ' shift into 8 hours ' work, 2 hours ' rest and 2 hours respectively violated the provisions of the and the Minimum Wages (Central) Rules 1950 and that the so called period of rest was illusory since being variable, it was some times given right at the commencement of the shift and some times at the end depending on the tides or the exigencies of the work. The workmen contended that regard being had to the number of actual work hours, the case of shore staff at the Weekly day could not be compared with that of the crew at that time. Held, that the provisions Of section 13 fixed the number and the number for any day and work up to 9 hours on any day can be spread over 12 hours and the extra hours will necessarily be hours of work of rest. The workers at the Alex andra Dock get a specified interval of one hour for rest and this makes up their 9 hours which is 8 hours work and one hour interval for rest. They are, therefore, entitled to three hours ' overtime if required to work beyond the 9 hours in any day.

The appellant was the tenant of a shop and the suit property was let out on June 25, 1976. The accommodation was for the first time assessed for house tax by the Nagar Palika Ghaziabad with effect from October 1, 1976, but as the assessment was made on October 1 1976, the provisions of U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 came to an end. The appellant filed a suit for eviction after termination of tenancy before the trial court and objection was raised that as the shop and basement were separately let out the tenancy could not be terminated by a single notice that would be invalid. The trial court dismissed the suit. The High Court set aside this conclusion of the trial Court, but allowed the revision petition filed by the appellant. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 2(2) of the U. P. Urban Building (Regulation) Act 1972 defines a "tenant" to mean any person who is in occupation or has been in occupation of any building for a continuous period of five years. The words "any person in occupation" and "any other person in possession" are defined in Section 2 (g) of that Act. [164A B] 1.2 In the instant case, the suit was filed within 10 years and therefore restriction as provided for in Section 20 can not be attracted. [165C D] 1:3 The appellant has been carrying out the business in the premises for a long time for it would be proper to permit the appellant time to make their arrangements for shifting. In default the respondent shall be entitled to execute the decree forthwith. [166E F] 1 :4. The suit was instituted within 10 year and therefore, restriction as per Section 20 is concerned they will not apply and therefore it is clear that during the pendency of the litigation even of 10 years expired the restriction will not be applicable and it is thus clear that in the instant appeal, even this contention of the appellant could not he accepted.

The appellant filed a suit for ejectment of three persons, namely Abdul Rahim, Abdul Hamid and Abdul Gaffur, from the property in suit (a parcel of land about 1 cottah 8 chittaks being part of premises No. 6 /1 Shibtola Lane), Khatian No. 7/1, Shibtla Road, Calcutta. In the notice to quit served on the 7th May, 1948, the first two persons were described as tenants under the plaintiff and the third as a person who had purported to purchase the structures on the land and the tenancy right therein. The suit was contested only by the third defendant who filed a written statement in September 1948 contending that the suit was bad for non joinder of parties. The trial court held that at the time when the appeal of the defendant was disposed of by the Subordinate Judge, the rights of the parties were governed by the Thika Tenancy Act of 1949 and the definition of thika tenant in that Act was not such as to afford any protection to the appellant. On a consideration of the provisions of the Act and Ordinance, the Subordinate judge held that the appellant was not liable to ejectment in the absence of any grounds therefor in the notice. The High Court on appeal by certificate granted a certificate of fitness under article 133(1)(c) of the Constitution. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that (i) the suit being bad for want of joinder, the respondent had to establish that he was entitled to possession because of the existence of any of the grounds mentioned in section 3; and (ii) the question whether section 4 of the Calcutta Thika tenancy Act, 1949 as amended by the Ordinance of 1953, is prospective or not. HELD: (i)(a) The legislature limited the applicability of the statute only to suits and appeals pending on 21st October 1952 and not in February, 1949 i.e., the date of the commencement of the Ordinance. It may be because before the Ordinance was promulgated no one could establish his rights as a thikatenant in view of the vague definition of "thika tenant" in the Act of 1948 which led to the decisions of the High Court against persons who sought to establish their rights as such. [184 D E] (b) The correct view is that sections 4 and 5 being prospective and as such inapplicable to pre Act suits, the landlord had to prove the existence thereof at the hearing of the suit, he had to consider whether any of these grounds in section 4 was available to him. [185 F] (c) Section 28 was meant to give relief to a thikika tenant who in a case where a decree or order for recovery of possession of any holding from a th kika tenant had been made before the date Of commencement of that Act. The controller in his turn had to deal with all pre suits on the basis that no notice under section 4 had been necessary.

The appellants were in the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as against the pay scales of Rs,120 300 to Section Officers. In 1965 the State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers and Rs. 150 350 for Section Officers, but it suggested that ten posts of Bench Secretaries should be upgraded and placed in the Pay scale ofRs. 2000 1,000 as recommended by the Pay Commission. The appellants filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order dated July 2, 1976. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the State Govern ment had granted uniform pay scale to both the grades of Bench Secretary and Section Officers in view of their differential duties. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the Pay Reti tion Committee did not accept the claim of Bench Ministers for giving them pay scales equal to Section officers or Private Secretaries; (2) the creation of two Grades with different pay scales in the cadre of Bench Stenographers who were doing the same or similar work and responsibilities there cannot be two grades with different Pay scales. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The Pay Commission refused to equate Bench Secretaries with Section Officers for equal work. It is found that the nature of duties and responsibilities of the two posts are quite different and more onerous than that Of Bench Secretaries. [306G] 2. The pay scale recommended by a Pay Commission was as follows: "Bench Secretary 26.38 Fifty two posts of Benches are in thepay scale of pay Rs.400750 and ten posts in the scale of RS.500 1,00000. The minimum pay scales is comparatively higher than the pay Scale of Upper Division Assistants though they were appointed through a competitive examination. The work of the Bench Secretary is of a great importance. [307A] 3. The Court Secretaries Grade I are selected among the lot of Bench Judges Grade II. When Benches Grade II acquire experience and also display more merit, they are appointed as Bench Secretaries Grade 1. When Bench Secretaries grade II acquired experience and even display more merits, they were appoint ed as Bench Secretary Grade I. [308B] 4. The rules thus make a proper classification for the purpose of entitlement to higher pay scale. The classification made under the Rules, therefore cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for equal Work.[307C D] 5. The principle of "equal pay for Equal work" has to be construed in the first place. Functions may be the same but the responsibilities make a difference. One cannot deny that often the difference is a matter of degree and that there is an element of value judgment by those who are charged with the administration in fixing the scales of pay and other conditions of service. So long as such value judgment emphasise that equal payfor equal work is a concomitant of Article 14 of the Constitution, but this principle naturally follows that equal Pay for equal duty will be a negation of that right. And said: "The same amount of physical work may entail different quality of work, some more sensitive. some requiring more tact, some less it varies from nature and culture of employment. If it has a rational nexus with the object to be sought for, as reiterated before a certain amount of value Judgment of the administrative authorities who are charge sheeted with fixing the payscales has to he left with them and it cannot be interfered with by the Court unless it is demonstrated that either it is irrational or based on no basis or arrived mala fide either in law or in fact. [309D E] 6. The State Government has granted uniform Pay scale scale of `Pay Rs. 1600 2950 to both these grades of Judges with effect from January 1, 1986.

The appellant company was incorporated under the , the entire share capital being owned by the Government of India. Powers were conferred on the Special Area Development Authority to impose property tax on lands and buildings within their jurisdiction. The procedure for imposition of taxes is contained in section 129 of the Municipalities Act and section 133 of the Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. By section 1(2) of that Act, the provisions inserted in the Municipalities (Amendment) Act 1976 were deemed to have come into force with effect from April 1, 1976. On June 24, 1976 respondent 1 made a further demand of Rs. 11 The appellant Company disputed its liability to pay the aforesaid amounts on the grounds, inter alia, that no tax was leviable on its property since the company was owned wholly by the government of India and that respondent I was estopped from levying the property tax by reason of the agreement of 1976. The first contention of the Attorney General was that respondent 1 could exercise only such powers to levy property tax as the Municipal Council or the Municipal council had under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 or the Madhya Bharat Municipalities Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the appellant company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that since the appellant companies were wholly owned by Government of india and that Respondent 1 was estopped by reason thereof, the property taxes imposed on them must be taken to have been incorporated in section 69(d) of the Act of 1973 and any subsequent change in those provisions by amendment of the two Acts cannot be availed of by respondent 1. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (1) The object behind the declaration contained in Section 2 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957 is not in any manner defeated by the legitimate exercise of taxing power under section 69 (d) or by the State Legislature. [16C] (2) The legislative field covered by Entry 23 of List II will pass on to Parliament by virtue of Entry 54, List I. But in order to 20 judge whether, on that account, the State legislature loses its competence to pass the Act, it is necessary to have regard to the object and purpose of that legislation and to the relevant provisions thereof, under which Special Area development Authorities are given the power to tax lands and building within their Jurisdiction. [17D] (3) The true effect behind the declarations contained in s 2 of Mines and Mineral (Regulation & Development)Act, 1957, is not the same thing as that of section 127A of the Madhya pradesh Municipalities Act which provides that property tax shall be paid primarily by the owner. It is true that on account of the declaration made by Parliament in respect of a declared industry and that the State Government had no competence to enact the impugned law by reason or Entry 52, List 1 read with Entry 24, List II.

The appellant was the lessee of a slate quarries in Venkatagiri. The lease was for a period exceeding one year and it was not enforceable against the Government, according to the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order declaring that the lease to the appellant had been granted subsequent to July 1, 1945, and that as the lease was only for a limited period exceeding two years it was no enforceable against it. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination of the appellant 's lease by the order dated December 27, 1955 was bad as it did not give three months notice to the lessee or provide for any compensation as required by section 20 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) The scheme of the impugned Act is to render ineffective all rights created after July 1 1945 for a Period exceeding one years and in one view of the matter it may well be taken as meaning that the creation of rights after July I 1945 is by the force of the second Proviso itself void as against the government without any further necessity for any overt act to be done by the Government to avoid the same. But assuming that the effect of the first proviso is to make the rights created before July 1 9, 1945 only voidable and not void, all that follows is that the Government must do something to avoid them. If the third proviso at all applied to rights created thereafter, then the second clause would be otiose and need not have been enacted at all. [560 D E] (ii) The words "such right " refer in the second sub section only to the right dealt with in the body of the section, and those words occurring in the third sub proviso should also bear the same interpretation. Under the second provisos leases for a periods exceeding one ye years and created after 1st July 1945, are not enforceable under the third clause. [561 F] (iii) The final step in the argument is that since the creation Of rights after 7th July 1 was void, it could only be done under the second part of section 20.
